text:
Today, @category_xyz is sharing the full whitepaper for Monad Private Settlement Domains (MPSDs)

Quick summary:
* transactions encrypted for the domain, ordered by Monad
* operators execute in Monad’s order; no separate domain consensus
* operators submit attestations and state commitments to Monad
* contracts exchange asynchronous messages across private domains and with public Monad
* contract access rules written in Solidity

MPSDs position Monad for a future where institutions move more of their financial operations onchain. Those institutions will need privacy and control, alongside access to shared liquidity and other applications.

The design puts Monad at the center of that activity. Institutions run their applications privately while using the public network for transaction ordering and settlement.

We are building for where institutional demand is heading, so Monad can support that growth while delivering the best of all worlds between privacy, compliance, and composability.

Whitepaper link in the next tweet

text:
Equity perpetuals are here: Americans can now trade perpetual futures on individual stocks listed on U.S. exchanges for the first time.

The @CFTC deemed the contracts approved as security futures, which the CFTC and @SECGov regulate jointly. U.S. investors get the protections of both agencies, the oversight Congress intended when it created a dedicated regime for security futures products.

In our August comment letter, we made the case that security futures treatment is the best path for these markets to flourish. Both CFTC- and SEC-regulated exchanges can list security futures, so venues primarily overseen by either agency can compete to offer this new class of product. That competition will improve outcomes for investors.

Equity perpetuals expand the tools that market participants can use to manage risk and take positions on securities in a single contract that never expires. We commend the staff of both agencies for this milestone in our derivatives markets.
author: aaalex
quoted_text:
Today, equity perps can begin trading for the first time on @CFTC registered exchanges.

This move reflects my commitment to ensuring that America’s markets remain the most innovative, liquid, and well-regulated in the world. Instead of being forced to turn to offshore, unregulated venues to access equity perpetual futures, Americans may now access equity perps on CFTC-regulated markets subject to robust safeguards.

I appreciate the continued partnership of @SECGov and @SECPaulSAtkins as we work to further harmonize our agencies' regulatory initiatives.

text:
Here's how to understand the CFTC equity perp news, simplified:

The @CFTC has approved equity perp contracts for the 4 exchanges that have filed requests to approve them:

- KalshiEX LLC
- Coinbase Derivatives
- Bitnomial (Kraken)
- Nadex/OG.com 

All 4 of these exchanges are:
1. CFTC registered exchanges
2. DCMs that clear trades with registered DCOs
3. Also registered with the SEC
4. That previously filed requests for approval of equity-perp contracts. 

The 4 exchanges have internal standards (which they've formalized and filed with the CFTC) for which equity-perp they can list on their own exchange. 

Things like 
- Equity is publicly traded
- Sufficient float, trading volume
- Reliable pricing to be able to calc funding payments
- Market structure resilient to manipulation

So the exchanges are *mostly* free to self-certify the markets they want, i.e. all the popular ones. Which is bullish, because we're about to get a lot of onshore equity perps available on US retail platforms like Coinbase, Kraken. 

btw, @Lighter_xyz will file with the @CFTC this month (per their Q3 investor call) and will very likely be the 5th exchange on this list (and the only crypto-native DEX with a CFTC DCM/DCO license), and is one of the reasons why Lighter is so unique as a project

text:
Darkbloom just passed 1 trillion tokens processed :)

I haven't tweeted much recently or shared many charts. We've been heads down on the thing that matters most right now: getting providers more work and better earnings.

Honestly, it's been a hard stretch. Provider earnings have been low. People trusted us with their machines and their time, and we take that seriously.

Inference keeps getting cheaper as architectures improve and more supply comes online. That means more people can use AI, but it also makes the economics harder for our providers. We have to keep finding where these machines can be most useful.

The mission is still the same: bring together all the spare compute out there and make it easy to own & share AI. I believe in that more than when we started.

And there's a lot more these machines can do.

More agents means more code to run, more tests, more builds. All those actions need compute too. Apple has built some incredibly capable, energy-efficient CPUs, and we want to put them to work.

We've started the private beta for Darkbloom Sandboxes and CI/CD.

We're starting with our own pipelines, cutting our internal costs by 50% while leaving healthy margins for providers. This gives us another way to bring useful, paying work to the network.

If you're looking for Mac CI or sandboxes, let us know. We'd love to work with you.

We're also continuing to push on inference. There's a lot of work going into open-source clustering on top of MLX; huge kudos to @Spangler3000 and @TheDavidTai for absolutely killing it on that front and writing SOTA for  models such as GLM 5.3 Flash.

I'm attaching the debrief @0xkydo shared with providers last week. He laid out the difficult parts openly, and how people responded meant a lot to me. Seeing people care this much about making it work, especially through a hard stretch, reminds me why I love building this.

It's a hard problem. We're going to keep attacking it. Thank you to everyone who have been here in this journey and continuing to support & be with us.

author: teortaxesTex
quoted_text:
We introduce Depth Hybrid Attention (DHA), which incorporates depth-wise value mixing into hybrid architectures with very little additional compute and cache overhead. By allowing layers to mix information across depth, DHA broadens each layer’s view and increases the model’s expressive capacity.

Our DHA method adapts to multiple hybrid architectures, including Depth Window Attention (DWA) for GQA + SWA and Depth Delta Attention (DDA) for MLA + KDA.

Across loss curves, short-context benchmark results, and long-context retrieval evaluations, both variants outperform their corresponding full-attention and hybrid-attention baselines, while retaining hybrid attention’s low KV-cache footprint.

text:
Garry Tan reveals why Y Combinator decides in just 10 minutes whether or not to fund a founder 

"The wild thing about Y Combinator is that we get 80,000, maybe 90,000 applications a year now for about 800 spots. So it is less than a 1% acceptance rate. Maybe 8 to 10% of those people would get an interview, sometimes less now." 

"And the wild thing is we actually spend only 10 minutes with them for that final stage."

"Paul Graham, the founder of YC, figured out that you didn't need half an hour, you don't need an hour. And then you could probably actually do it in about 5 minutes, but 5 minutes feels rude. So that's how YC ended up at 10 minutes."

"It sounds almost too simple, but 10 minutes is a wonderful constraint. Like how 140 characters for Twitter way back in the day was a wonderful constraint. If you can say something very simply that hits us, here's a user, here's a real person who has a problem, and here's how the technology that we build actually solves that. We just want to know what it is and why it's awesome."

"And then if we have a little bit of extra time, we want to know why that founder is the person to go and build that thing. And you can do all of that in 10 minutes. And it's an up-down decision." 

"Something like 10% to 15% of all self-made billionaires as of now, aged 50 and under, are YC alums."

Walter Isaacson: "Let's say Elon Musk, he walked in and you had 10 minutes with him. What do you think the percentage chance is that you would actually fund him?"

Garry Tan: "100%. In current form, 100%. I had a managing partner meeting the other day, and that's actually one of the example questions we ask ourselves to figure out whether we're on the right track." 

"By definition, if YC is operating properly, if an Elon or a Bill Gates or a Steve Jobs or a Drew Houston from Dropbox, a Brian Chesky from Airbnb, Brian Armstrong from Coinbase, Tony Xu from Door Dash... if someone like that walks into our office, can we say yes to them in 10 minutes? And if that answer is no, actually I'd have to rewrite everything. We'd have to retool everything. That is almost the only question that really matters when it comes to whether YC is doing well or not."

text:
People who only look at tokenomics will keep getting crypto investing very wrong.

I still see people comparing $AERO and $UNI, completely missing why UNI’s valuation is so much higher.

Uniswap is a fully decentralized protocol deployed across multiple chains. It’s practically synonymous with DeFi and token swaps.

Now look at Aerodrome.

There’s Coinbase, a centralized exchange. They built their own centralized database using Ethereum technology (Base L2), then boosted DEX on top of it.

Now that DEX is trying to expand to other chains by throwing rewards and inflation.

And all of this runs on ve(3,3) tokenomics, with token locking, which I consider far inferior to a straightforward buyback-and-burn model.

That’s why the valuations are so different.

Make your own choice.

text:
Thoughts from my Shanghai field trip

Sentiment among Greater China investors was far worse than I expected. Unlike the US market, A shares had not seen a single rebound since July. Still holding Chinese and Hong Kong AI stocks that had crashed and Korean memory stocks that had collapsed, investors kept pressing me on when memory would bounce back.

Many investors said the AI trade was over, and a few said they doubted whether even 2027 capex, not just 2028, would go ahead as planned.

Overall, the bearish sentiment was so strong that even I, a bull before coming to China, started to waver.

It got to the point where, faced with the bear case that memory prices could start falling in the third quarter of next year, I took it seriously and couldn't refute it.

As the conversations went on, I gradually began to understand where their pessimism was coming from. In the end, they were all asking the same question.

So what comes after AI coding? What will be the next engine of ARR for Anthropic and OpenAI?

Several candidates came up. AI4S, AI chip design, and so on... But none of them clearly convinced investors.

I couldn't offer a clear answer either. Sure, there are rumors that Anthropic has made major breakthroughs in both AI4S and AI chip design, but what we actually want to know is when any of that turns into money.

With AI4S, there could be beneficiaries right away, such as companies that sell lab monkeys or diagnostic kits. In fact, there already are. But while we can trade those names in the short term, what we ultimately want to know is whether Anthropic can make money by developing drugs. That is still several years away.

As for AI chip design, the TAM itself is hard to calculate, and even if you do calculate it, it is hard to monetize. That makes it difficult for the market to believe in.

Honestly, this feels like the hardest market in history. If a company isn't making money, selling makes sense. But right now the market sells even when companies are making money, even when they beat, and even when they say demand will stay solid all the way through 2028 and 2029.

So my recommendation to investors was to buy memory, and within memory, DRAM. Not because I have conviction in the DRAM cycle, but because I see it as a relatively defensive choice within the AI trade.

Memory stocks are now trading close to 1x P/B on 2027 BPS. Historically, memory stocks have staged technical rebounds when they fell below 1x P/B.

And even if the broader market falls further from here, the three DRAM makers will keep buying back their own shares. I thought that would guarantee a certain level of buying and concluded the stocks would have downside support.

Of course, I don't know whether memory stocks can break above their previous highs. That depends on whether sentiment across the broader market recovers. But I think there is a fairly good chance that memory outperforms the rest of the AI trade.

text:
OpenAI 应用 AI 工程负责人 Wulfie Bain 在 X 上发帖，教想加入自己团队的求职者写简历，总结成四条：

1. 写短
2. 删掉无关经历
3. 写成果，不只写做了什么
4. 让人能快速扫到重点

Bain 在 OpenAI 带领面向创业公司的应用 AI 工程团队。之前自己创过业，当过CTO，毕业于牛津大学。更早在波士顿咨询公司（BCG）做过招聘。

Bain 说自己前后看过几千份简历，所以这些建议对咨询等其他行业也适用。

这是 Bain 关于申请 OpenAI 的系列帖第三篇，团队还有新职位即将开放。

讲建议之前，Bain 先说了两点。

第一，能找到内推最好。
内推就是由公司内部认识你的员工把你推荐给招聘方。没有熟人就只能网上投递，Bain 自己就是在网上投简历进的 OpenAI。

第二，简历没法完整展现一个人。
它的作用是证明你有相关经验、能把事情讲清楚，让招聘方愿意约你聊一次。

四条建议具体是这样：

1. 写短。
最好一页，但内容是否相关比硬凑页数更重要。简历本身就在展示你会不会写、懂不懂取舍。

2. 删掉无关经历。
每条经历都要写清楚跟这份工作有什么关系，不相关的就删。Bain 举例说，自己也为高中时的成绩骄傲，但现在找工作时它们通常用不上。

3. 写成果，不只写动作。
只写做了什么，读的人看不出这件事值不值得做。Bain 的例子是：只写"重新设计了一个 AI 智能体的架构"（智能体指能自动完成任务的 AI 程序），说明不了价值；写"把响应时间缩短 2 秒，客户满意度因此提高"，才是成果。做销售的，就写带来了多少收入。

4. 方便快速浏览。
把重要内容加粗，每段经历下把最有说服力的证据放在第一条。招聘方要在一大堆简历里很快判断该约谁面试。

Bain 说，表达清楚、经历相关、拿得出成果，这三点在整个申请过程中都重要。后续还会继续发建议。

author: Jack24klove
quoted_text:
About 3,600 SOL from the Binance theft reached a HitBTC @hitbtc hot wallet at 08:51 UTC on November 3, after being routed through multiple paths using automated scripts and a peeling-chain pattern.   

Once again, HitBTC has surfaced in the laundering trail of a major crypto theft.  

As we previously reported, roughly $22M in illicit funds had flowed into HitBTC by July this year. https://t.co/dVLQEUHTQI 

In the $1.4B Bybit hack, at least $3.68M linked to North Korean money-laundering networks also reached the platform. Bybit’s subsequent requests for assistance with its investigation were met with little response.  

Hackers often rely on nested services to launder stolen funds. HitBTC has featured in these arrangements across multiple cases, frequently serving as a key link in DPRK's laundering operations.  

Nested services—such as instant swap providers, smaller exchanges, and OTC desks—connect to larger platforms via APIs to access their liquidity.   

On-chain activity reveals only the platform’s addresses. The platform’s internal records identify the intermediary, while the actual end user remains hidden one layer deeper.

text:
Just finished our first roundtable at the prediction market hub! One down five more to go 😅

Rather than talks, we preferred a more interactive approach that leveraged the intelligence of all attendees. Talks can be seen on YouTube, but different projects sharing their learnings with each other can only happen irl

The following points were discussed in the roundtable;

1. The biggest target for growth in PMs is going after the insurance market. 

Although @clesaege pointed out it's utility is in discovering odds rather than directly doing insurance, as providers get leverage over multiple claims while PMs are only on each market. Prediction markets evolving into decentralized insurance was a promising avenue

Another avenue for prediction markets is ofc decision making , esp with AI making the cost of submitting so cheap, markets can help with filtering. The hardest part of getting such markets off the ground is simply the absence of existing traders, for eg there are people whose job is predicting bitcoin daily price but no trader whose job is estimating flight delays or chances of a candidate getting the job

2. The other part revolved around manipulation in prediction markets, which take the following forms

a. Insider trading in markets which prevents real traders or speculators from participating, as they know the odds are stacked against them 

b. Resolution criteria or oracles being flawed

c. Reality benders who put money in an outcome only to increase its probability. For eg, as a democrat supporter you can either donate or put money in the PM to boost their odds

Some egs discussed were the the Brazilian election where over 80%  predicted bolsonaro, but then he lost - wa that an oracles issue or just market being inefficient?

3. And finally we discussed different prediction market structures. Currently we just have binary markets which settle to 0 or hero; the main question to figure out is whether that's the final form of prediction markets or a temporary phase

One trader said he wanted scalar prediction markets for  markets on bitcoin price that pay out based on how close you were to the price, rather than just a dumb 0 if below threshold or 1 if above

I also learnt about directional markets for the 1st time. We concluded by talking about conditional markets (for eg odds of democrats winning the presidency if Biden is nominee vs Harris)

Combining several conditional markets can help make them capital efficient, since only the market actually resolving will determine profit and loss . So if you put money on republican odds if trump nominee and democrats if Biden is nominee, your P&L across both markets is based only on the trump market

Overall really looking forward to going deep into the prediction market world next 3 days to advance the state of the art, it's cool that we have traders, customers, prediction market platforms all under the same tent to share learnings with one another

Meanwhile, their machines are supposed to be monitored closely physically during working time and not supposed to be used to access critical cluster off work. Probably most of devs are working remotely, but for the critical access must require "multi-approval" via online meeting to ensure security. @cz_binance @heyibinance

The attacks are no longer protectable by smart contract audit or typical blockchain security, but requires deep-infra experts at CTO level that understands the entire workflow and knows the bolts and nuts of how the complex system works in happy path/corner cases.

It's a huge challenge for SMEs and even big companies like @binance , but it's becoming common practice in post-AGI era. No bullet proof, have to constantly learn and apply patches.

5）故技重施，HLP 被迫接管 1200 万「弃子」多仓

16 地址集群抽离保证金，HLP 接管逾 1200 万美元多仓，本轮 XPL 闪崩发生于 11 月 1 日 12:32，当分钟价格从开盘至最低下跌约 18%

据 Quote 流动性供应商复盘，16 地址集群此前合计持有约 2309 万美元 XPL 多仓，其中 12 个地址在暴跌前集中提交并获准约 203.86 万美元提现请求

Hyperliquid 官方成交记录显示，HLP 清算金库在本轮事件中合计接管约 1217.7 万美元 XPL 多仓，涉及 30 个遭清算账户，其中 11 个属于上述集群。Quote 测算最终处置损失约 55.58 万美元

这类被称为「自杀式清算」的交易结构，通常表现为账户在保留大额多仓的同时，提前提走可提现保证金，压缩剩余仓位的清算缓冲

此类操作的潜在获利来源可能来自 CEX 现货与合约市场的配合。若相关账户同时在中心化交易所持有空头头寸，或通过现货交易参与价格波动，其跨市场收益可能覆盖 Hyperliquid 多仓的清算损失。尤其当大额仓位被动平仓加剧价格下跌时，其他市场的空头可能获得收益，而部分流动性不足的残余仓位风险则由 HLP 承接

Today, @category_xyz is sharing the full whitepaper for Monad Private Settlement Domains (MPSDs)

Quick summary:
* transactions encrypted for the domain, ordered by Monad
* operators execute in Monad’s order; no separate domain consensus
* operators submit attestations and state commitments to Monad
* contracts exchange asynchronous messages across private domains and with public Monad
* contract access rules written in Solidity

MPSDs position Monad for a future where institutions move more of their financial operations onchain. Those institutions will need privacy and control, alongside access to shared liquidity and other applications.

The design puts Monad at the center of that activity. Institutions run their applications privately while using the public network for transaction ordering and settlement.

We are building for where institutional demand is heading, so Monad can support that growth while delivering the best of all worlds between privacy, compliance, and composability.

Whitepaper link in the next tweet

AirBnB just started  offering weather Prediction Markets to it's users.

Users can hedge bad weather at their destination by betting on rain levels.

this is a trillion dollar usecase.

here is how it works:

- users choose to pay a small "insurance fee" (stake) when booking
- payout is determined automatically based on the odds of rain
- If it rains, payout is automatically credited to their account

No claim, No verification, 100% automated.

Essentially, this is a prediction market bet disguised as insurance.

This is called a "Parametric insurance".

And it's what will take prediction markets from the $600B gambling industry to the $8T insurance industry.

Right now AirBnB is settling the bet through Chubb, a legacy insurance company, but they explicitly do NOT disclose their oracle anywhere.

I wouldn't be surprised if they were already using @Kalshi behind the scenes.

It would be incredibly easy for them to use Kalshi to :
- receive accurate weather odds
- handle market resolution
- even settle payouts

All the insurer would do is charge a premium over the odds and collect the difference.

If this usecase takes on, @Kalshi & @Polymarket could become the backbone of a trillion dollars industry.

text:
I constantly find myself reminding people just because AI is dropping the cost of building software to zero doesn’t mean you should default to building everything.

People are trigger happy when it comes to build vs. buy without fully considering the opportunity cost of their time & cognitive load.

My general rule of thumb is to focus build resources on 3 things:

1) Core processes or product that maintain or extend your edge. Example: for stitch fix their styling and recommendation algorithms; for an insurance co, their risk models for underwriting 

2) Owning your context. This doesn’t mean you need to own the models and it also doesn’t mean you need to own the plumbing. It means you do need to capture and organize your tribal knowledge + the eval data. 

3) Huge cost dislocations where the ROI of ripping a vendor out and replacing it with a build hits an internally assigned threshold

author: varun_mathur
quoted_text:
🖖 Introducing EdgeLLama - An Open Standard for Decentralized AI 
           
We, the GPU poor, have come up with a peer-to-peer network design to enable running Mistral7B and other models which will make AI use more free, both as in beer and as in speech. We believe in e/acc, and we want to make AI abundant. This is the moment in time, when we start taking back control from the few powerful AI companies. 

Right now, our AI use is a function of expensive monthly subscriptions, rate and usage limits imposed by datacenter-cloud run AI companies. This gives them the power to decide what we can prompt with and how much of AI we even have access to. The immense power they wield also imposes an emotional burden on them, and they are trying to appeal to the government to now impose stifling regulations (a concept called "regulatory capture", see @bgurley's talk). 

Well, we, a bunch of AI and open network aficionados, want to make their lives' easier and take that power away from them. Think BitTorrent from the early 2000s, when you could make your own computer available and effortlessly share files with each other in an open network. The advent of that technology, which was used by over 100 million people running nodes on their home computers, imposed a forcing function on entertainment business models in general. Better user experiences emerged, providing unlimited access to top-tier content for an insanely low fees. 

EdgeLLama, and the associated set of products, which lead to a seamless AI consumer-cloud will impose a similar abundant forcing function on AI as well. You can go ahead and cancel your $20/month Pro plans, because this next wave of AI, runs in your laptops, desktops and smartphones, and is good enough. 

There is an active, growing community of true open AI advocates: releasing foundation models, making them easier to run on regular laptops and curating datasets - we are supplementing that world with the just right peer-to-peer network design and the just right UX along with it. In the earlier post we shared how AI, with community curated datasets leads to better and more credible responses than some of the top closed AI companies. In this post, we outline an early draft of network design and a look at the EdgeLlama node software which you can run on your device - serving inference and vectors to the community. You will simply earn good karma, and nothing more, but you will sleep better at night, knowing that you served AI for some student in Mumbai or reasonable medical advice for someone in Manila.. 

• What is EdgeLLama ? 
It is both an open protocol, and also the name of the software you can install on your computer which will enable you to serve AI for others in either your chosen community (eg, "Stanford" or "astrophysics"), or the wider world, and on the flip side, also benefit from it. 

• How is this different from local desktop software already available ? 
They are local only. EdgeLLama is a peer-to-peer network. It is going to be necessary for hosting a world of millions of community-finetuned LLMs, running across a shared vector pool (more on that in our next post..).

• How do I run EdgeLlama on my computer ? 
It will be available sometime next week. Please join this TG group if you are interested in running a node: https://t.co/EKlAomD6na 

• Any restrictions on which UIs and models it can work with ? 
No, we do not care - our focus here is on UX. We will provide an integration with Collama's web user interface, and also with some recent popular models which can run on your devices (such as Mistral7B, Llama2 and others) - but you should be able to run/modify EdgeLLama as you want. We seek to encourage a diverse set of clients which implement the EdgeLLama protocol.

• Will there be an API ?
Yes. As a developer, you will be able to default to using the EdgeLLama consumer network in co-ordination with your users, instead of paying for GPU in datacenters only. 

• Wait - so I can get better results than top AI companies and also get them for free ?
Yes - that is the plan. Using Collama's trusted community dataset approach (think Wikipedia-style millions of finetuned community LLMs) leads to better results, and using EdgeLLama leads to reducing the cost of running AI and provides more freedom. 

• Does this use cryptography ? 
Yes, we use public key cryptography and other mechanisms for fundamental trusted operation of the system. These are defined in detail in the early draft of the paper below. 

• Do you use advanced cryptography like ZKML or FHE ? 
We seek to support teams building ZKML sub-networks on EdgeLLama. However, we believe using this needs to be a function of user choice, given the trade-offs in cost and complexity involved. In addition to eventual fully trusted running of models, we anticipate few years from now with advanced cryptography concepts like FHE being able to scale, the security and ability to work on fully encrypted data at scale will only grow and reach viability. However, keep in mind that even though ZK proofs were invented in 1984, they weren't even used for Bitcoin to start with. Sometimes the most exciting technology has the longest arc, and what people want are practical solutions they can start using today. 

• Is this decentralized ? 
Yes. Over a period of time, a fully permissionless protocol also becomes available for those who choose it.

• Does this use a blockchain ? 
No, while this is decentralized, and uses a mechanism to reasonably filter out malicious nodes, it does not use a blockchain. 

• Will there be a blockchain protocol ? 
Yes, think Bitcoin, but for AI. We expect 99% of the EdgeLLama node providers here will simply run the non-crypto base software, while 1% of the node providers might choose to participate in an optional staking protocol to provide a higher quality of service for block rewards. That 1% will fund the infrastructure and continuous development of the entire network.

• What are you: an AI or a blockchain project ? 
At Hyperspace (@HyperspaceAI), we are building the world's largest decentralized AI network which uses 21st century economics to incentivize the servicing of that network, beyond just a feeling of social good. Advent of BitTorrent, Bitcoin, and the economic principles of Ethereum have taught us useful lessons. We view both blockchains and AI as simply data compression engines and replicated state machines, which need to entirely run on regular user devices. The peer-to-peer network here amongst laptops, desktops and smartphones is going to enable a new type of a supercomputer, on which a variety of society advancing technologies will run, some yet to be invented. 

What we seek to build here is an open movement. These are the earliest, chaotic, raw days - and perhaps the best time to start collaborating together. 

-----------------------------------------------------------

📄 EdgeLLama: An Open Standard For Distributed Inference In Federated Networks     

Here is a look at an early snippet of the EdgeLLama paper. The phase 1 of this decentralized AI network uses community servers for co-ordination between nodes and phase 2 will provision a fully peer-to-peer, permissionless protocol.

1. Introduction
==============
EdgeLLama is an open standard designed to allow any supported machine to serve as an inference provider. It's a stateful application layer communication protocol that offers HTTP and WebSocket APIs to securely transmit inference requests in JSON format across two primary layers: the CommunityServer-Edge Communication Layer and the CommunityServer-CommunityServer Communication Layer.

2. CommunityServer System Model
==============================

2.1 Community Cluster
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
The model presupposes an asynchronous distributed system. Within this system, nodes are interconnected through a network. It's acknowledged that this network might exhibit certain inefficiencies: it might not deliver messages, could delay, duplicate, or even rearrange them.

To safeguard the integrity of message transmission, we employ cryptographic measures. These measures include the integration of public-key signatures, message authentication codes, and digests generated by collision-resistant hash functions.

It is of utmost importance to ascertain that a received message genuinely emanates from a specified node, ensuring it hasn't been tampered with or fabricated by malevolent entities.

For achieving this on a Community Server, there are two potential implementations: stateful and stateless.

Under a stateful approach, an identity session is sustained for each EdgeLlama node on the Community Server. This implies the presence of data that mandates replication amongst Community Servers. This in turn necessitates either state machine replication amongst Community Servers or an auxiliary protocol facilitating communication, enabling Community Servers to mutually affirm the veracity of an authentication.

Considering a scenario with multiple Community Servers: CS 1, CS 2,... CS n. Should a novel node affiliate with a Community Server, and the identity of this node remains ambiguous to the server, it becomes essential for the Community Server to cross-verify with its peers. This is to determine if any of the other Community Server can vouch for the node's identity. This cross-verification is based on the authentication payload transmitted by the EdgeLlama node.

Combining digital signatures with message digests allows nodes to sign the digest of a message so that other nodes can verify both the integrity of the message and its origin without having to maintain any session key that requires a state entry in the Community Server. This basically means that an EdgeLlama node is identified by its public key throughout the network and due to the cryptographical primitives mentioned, it can sign and prove its authenticity throughout the network.

2.2 Model Registry
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Upon successfully establishing a connection to a Community Server, an EdgeLlama node communicates its capabilities. This encompasses details like the types of models it can execute (HuggingFace ID), the model's revision, quantization, CUDA support, and other pertinent characteristics. Given this information, the Community Server categorizes the EdgeLlama node, subscribing it to the relevant PubSub topic correlating with the model it operates on.

The fortification check is initiated once there have been 'n' successful inferences executed for an identical model. Subsequent to this, the Community Server focuses on maintaining the caliber of nodes associated with that topic. The Community Server prompts the EdgeLlama node with a number alpha of Inference Calls, chosen at random from the preceding 'n' successful inferences. As a reference, the Community Server retains the digests of the outputs from these inferences. Adhering to the protocol standard, the EdgeLlama node, given its subscription to the model's topic, executes the prescribed inference. Upon completion, a comparison is made between the digest of this recent inference and the stored digests within the Community Server. If there's a match, the Community Server is deemed to have successfully passed the fortification check.

2.3 Inference Event
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
The process of facilitating an inference is not merely a direct function call but a more orchestrated communication between the Community Server and the various EdgeLlama nodes.

When the Community Server receives an inbound request for inference, it primarily consists of two main components:
• Prompt: A string that delineates the information or data upon which the inference is to be executed.
• Model: A ModelConfig object that encapsulates the details of the model to be employed for the inference. The ModelConfig is expected to have specifics like the model's identifier, version, etc.

Upon receipt of the inference request, the Community Server's immediate task is to identify the set of EdgeLlama nodes that are capable of fulfilling the request. This is achieved by:
• Referencing the ModelConfig object within the request to identify the desired model.
• Consulting its internal registry to retrieve a list of EdgeLlama nodes that are subscribed to the identified model topic.

With the list of appropriate EdgeLlama nodes at its disposal, the Community Server commences the process of broadcasting the inference request. But before that, a "seed" and a "UUID" for that specific inference request is generated by the Community Server. The Community Server appends the seed and the ID to the inference request and the inference request is disseminated in parallel to a fanout of the identified EdgeLlama nodes. This ensures that multiple nodes have the opportunity to process the request, catering to redundancy and increasing the chances of a prompt response. Each EdgeLlama node, upon receiving the broadcasted request, will initiate the necessary steps to run the inference based on the provided prompt and its local instance of the model specified in the ModelConfig.

Given the deterministic execution nature of models in this specific environment, an identical outcome is expected when the same seed and model parameters are provided. The Community Server leverages this characteristic to assure the precision and uniformity of inferences.

2.4 Inference Aggregation
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Inference aggregation stands as a cardinal stage in the Community Server's inference process, especially in contexts endorsing distributed inference tasks spread across numerous EdgeLlama nodes.

The Community Server, by juxtaposing responses from diverse nodes, can isolate the most recurrent response, thereby amplifying the final outcome's accuracy. When certain EdgeLlama nodes encounter latency, discrepancies, or faults in their output, the strategy of dispersing the inference task across multiple nodes furnishes the Community Server with redundancy and alternative response routes. The employed aggregation methodology pivots around a simple majority vote paired with feedback loops. Viewing an Inference Resolution digest as a vote, the Community Server Protocol calculates a trustworthiness score for each unique response digest. Under standard conditions, a singular distinct response digest is anticipated from the EdgeLlama nodes. This trust score is derived using a weighted voting approach. Here, responses from particular EdgeLlama nodes, which have been historically reliable or have met specific criteria, carry added significance. The preferred response is the one that accumulates the maximum aggregated weight.

The implementation of a feedback loop is critical. Should specific EdgeLlama nodes recurrently yield aberrant or erroneous responses, the Community Server can activate a feedback mechanism. This may lead to recalibrations of the node's credibility score or potential flagging of the node for scrutiny.

Subsequently, the Community Server compiles the ultimate result, which could encompass: 
• Amalgamated inference outcome.
• Accompanying metadata: this might involve details such as the count of participating nodes, timestamps, signatures, and digests. For diagnostic purposes or ensuring transparency, the distinct outputs from the EdgeLlama nodes — inclusive of their signatures — may also be annexed, offering a comprehensive perspective on the aggregation phase...

Last night, my lawyers moved to sanction World Liberty Financial @worldlibertyfi for failing to disclose, until months into my litigation against the company, that it is a citizen of the UAE 🇦🇪 . #WLFI #USD1 

For those who are new to this dispute, I was one of World Liberty’s earliest and largest investors.  In November 2024, I agreed to buy $30 million of $WLFI tokens under a Token Purchase Agreement with World Liberty, and I later increased my total investment to $45 million. 

In April, I sued World Liberty, alleging that the company induced my investment through fraud and then unlawfully froze my tokens.

My Token Purchase Agreement gives me the right to bring my claims in either California federal or state court.  

I chose federal court.

Federal courts can hear a case like mine only when the two sides come from different places.  Foreign plaintiffs like me can sue an American defendant in federal court, but foreign plaintiffs generally cannot sue a foreign defendant there.  For these purposes, a company like World Liberty takes on the citizenship of each of its owners, so a single foreign owner makes the company foreign.  

In other words, so long as World Liberty and all of its owners were American, my case could be heard in federal court.

The federal court’s rules required World Liberty to file a disclosure at the start of the case identifying every one of its owners and where each is a citizen.  World Liberty’s disclosure identified only one entity—World Liberty itself—and listed Florida as its sole citizenship.  Its lawyers certified that they were unaware of anyone else who needed to be disclosed.

World Liberty then moved to compel arbitration, seeking to pull my case out of open court and into secret arbitration proceedings. 

I opposed that motion, and my lawyers spent months and hundreds of thousands of dollars fighting it.  At a hearing in August, the Court signaled that it was not persuaded that my claims belonged in arbitration.  Instead, the Court ruled that certain of my claims should stay in open court, and certain claims should be sent to arbitration, and ordered the parties to meet and confer to come up with a proposed agreement on which claims stay in open court and which ones go to arbitration.

Less than a week later, World Liberty suddenly “corrected” its disclosure.  Where it had previously listed only one member in its ownership chain, it now listed 22, and claimed citizenship in Florida, Delaware, Puerto Rico, and the UAE.  

World Liberty now says that the federal court has no jurisdiction over my case, since its UAE citizenship means there are foreign parties on both sides of the case.

The irony is hard to miss.  World Liberty’s gold paper declares that “[b]y design, World Liberty Financial is not organized offshore,” and that it is “an American, tax-paying, corporation that aims to bring DeFi to its rightful home—America.”  It promises a “US-based decentralized platform” built on “American ideals of liberty, privacy, and freedom to transact,” calls private, intermediary-free transactions “a core American value,” and boasts that “[r]ather than shying away from the United States, World Liberty Financial embraces the United States as the future CRYPTO CAPITAL OF THE PLANET.”

World Liberty was proudly American 🇺🇸 when it was selling tokens.  It discovered its UAE 🇦🇪 roots only when it needed a way out of an American federal courtroom.

World Liberty presumably always knew who its owners were.  Its lawyers claim that they learned about the company’s UAE citizenship only after they filed the original disclosure.  

As my motion explains, if that is true, then either World Liberty’s lawyers failed to conduct appropriate diligence, or World Liberty did not give its lawyers a straight answer.  When we asked how this happened, World Liberty refused to tell us.

Token holders deserve to know whether the projects they invest in are telling the truth, both to the public and to courts.  I am filing this motion to hold World Liberty and its lawyers accountable for what I believe was a misleading disclosure to the Court, and to make sure that the cost of World Liberty’s gamesmanship falls on them, not on me.  

And after my sanctions motion is resolved in federal court, I will re-file my lawsuit against World Liberty in California state court.

I will keep fighting for the transparency this community deserves.

text:
This is JP Morgan’s view is Wall Street consensus. It assumes there is one Democratic Party. 

My view aligns more with Democrat Strategist Jim Carville, who spoke on the Bulwark podcast two weeks ago. He suggests there are two Democratic parties, the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and the more moderate/traditional Democrats. These divisions mean the margin of victory might play a huge role in the market’s reaction.
--
Carville:
“I would be disappointed if it comes in at 225 House seats. That would almost be—I would rather the Republicans keep the House by five than the Democrats win by five because if that happens, they’re hostage to the DSA. Like, Hakeem [Jeffries] cannot move. He has nowhere to go. Even if you have a close Senate, [Sen. John] Fetterman would keep [Sen. Chuck] Schumer Pepto-Bismol all night. So I think this is one of those races where margin matters a lot.”
--

We would add that if the Senate is a 51-49 Democrat majority, not only does presumed Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer have to worry about PA Senator John Fetterman siding with Republicans, but Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders and a presumed Michigan winner Abdul El-Sayed could put up a “block” because the Democratic Party is not progressive enough.

This issue would come to a head almost immediately over data centers.

Moderate/traditional Democrats, such as unions and middle-class voters, want those jobs. They are accelerationists. 

The DSA wants to block more data center construction. They are decelerationists.

This could turn into an epic fight within the Democratic Party.

刚刚，Binance 官方正式发布了关于 10 月 29 日 63 亿美元被盗事件的初步调查报告。

结论显示，这并非一次简单的“私钥泄露”，而是朝鲜黑客（FBI 调查认为吻合）潜伏数月、策划的一场有预谋的攻击。

报告透露了几个实战关键细节：

1.极致的社工骗局，连“HR”的社交日常都是伪造的
黑客在 9 月通过正规招聘平台盯上了币安的软件工程师。为了诱敌深入，黑客不仅安排了“项目总监”和“CEO”的多轮视频面试，甚至在面试中主动分享虚假的社交媒体照片和视频来建立信任。
最终，他们成功诱导该工程师在面试后，给自己的工作电脑上下载了伪装成“面试作业”的 0-day 恶意软件。

2. 内部 AI 工具沦为黑客的“内网跳板”

黑客在控制了首个工程师的电脑后，竟然直接利用币安的“内部 AI 工具”作为横向移动的跳板，顺藤摸瓜控制了另一位拥有核心权限的钱包 DevOps 工程师的设备，最终拿到了容器部署权限。

3. EIP-7702 与 MPC 机制，被坏人利用

在 10 月 29 日的最终收网阶段，黑客极其狡猾地利用了以太坊的 EIP-7702 机制（允许账户将执行权委托给智能合约，而无需暴露私钥）。

更让人感到无奈的是，币安热钱包所采用的 MPC（多方安全计算）机制，原本是为了消除单点故障、提升安全性，却在黑客发难的紧急时刻成了限制因素；
因为“没有单一私钥”，安全团队无法一键撤销黑客的恶意授权，反而拉长了阻断攻击的时间。

看完这个官方的报告，小编的感觉只有用防不胜防来形容了。

视频面试做局、大厂AI工具当跳板、反向利用 MCP 机制来拖延时间，原有的每一个环节都以意想不到的方式被巧妙的利用起来。

整个行业的安全假设确实需要重新审视了。

The irony is hard to miss.  World Liberty’s gold paper declares that “[b]y design, World Liberty Financial is not organized offshore,” and that it is “an American, tax-paying, corporation that aims to bring DeFi to its rightful home—America.”  It promises a “US-based decentralized platform” built on “American ideals of liberty, privacy, and freedom to transact,” calls private, intermediary-free transactions “a core American value,” and boasts that “[r]ather than shying away from the United States, World Liberty Financial embraces the United States as the future CRYPTO CAPITAL OF THE PLANET.”

World Liberty was proudly American 🇺🇸 when it was selling tokens.  It discovered its UAE 🇦🇪 roots only when it needed a way out of an American federal courtroom.

World Liberty presumably always knew who its owners were.  Its lawyers claim that they learned about the company’s UAE citizenship only after they filed the original disclosure.  

As my motion explains, if that is true, then either World Liberty’s lawyers failed to conduct appropriate diligence, or World Liberty did not give its lawyers a straight answer.  When we asked how this happened, World Liberty refused to tell us.

Token holders deserve to know whether the projects they invest in are telling the truth, both to the public and to courts.  I am filing this motion to hold World Liberty and its lawyers accountable for what I believe was a misleading disclosure to the Court, and to make sure that the cost of World Liberty’s gamesmanship falls on them, not on me.  

And after my sanctions motion is resolved in federal court, I will re-file my lawsuit against World Liberty in California state court.

I will keep fighting for the transparency this community deserves.

text:
An announcement that is as personal as professional:

18 months ago, we started collecting online prices in real time to track how Liberation Day tariffs were feeding into inflation.

A lot has happened since. The BLS commissioner was fired. The longest government shutdown in US history meant CPI wasn’t published for the first time. And the case for an independent measure of inflation became much stronger.

What started as a tariff inflation tracker has since grown into something much bigger: 

The Bloomberg Price Project (BPP), our attempt to build the US CPI from the ground up using alternative data.

Today, BPP covers 87% of the CPI basket, across both goods and services (more new data will be added in coming weeks). Every month, we collect millions of prices from card transactions, e-commerce sites, grocery stores, pharmacies, rental listings, corporate data, Bloomberg Terminal market prices and government records. And more data are coming.

The payoff is detail. Official CPI data let you drill down to categories such as “uncooked beef steaks.” BPP goes much deeper — breaking the CPI basket into almost 700 line items, compared with roughly 200 in the official data.

Brought to you by: myself, Troy Durie, Daniel Ripperger-Suhler, Joshua Danial and Scott Johnson from across Bloomberg Economics.

Explore the Bloomberg Price Project at BECO MODELS BPP <GO>, or download the data at ECAN US BPI <GO>.

text:
A biologist in Ohio is living with a rare form of cystic fibrosis. His particular mutation is not amenable to existing drugs for the disease.

And that’s why, for the last 10+ years, he has been trying to make a gene therapy to cure it. New essay today in @AsimovPress.

Most people living with cystic fibrosis still make copies of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein. These proteins are often defective, but modern drugs can help them fold or function properly.

And these drugs have been enormously successful. For decades, treatments like antibiotics and mechanical vibration vests have helped clear bacteria from the airways and raise life expectancy for people with cystic fibrosis from about 10 years to 40. Newer drugs that restore CFTR function have pushed life expectancy even higher; many patients today can live relatively normal lives.

But about 5–10% of people with cystic fibrosis have mutations that prevent them from making essentially any CFTR protein at all. These are often called nonsense or frameshift mutations. And because these patients don't make the protein, the existing CFTR-modulating drugs have nothing to act upon.

@jacobwitten1, the author of today's essay, is one of these patients. His laboratory at Case Western Reserve University is developing lipid nanoparticles that can deliver RNA into lung cells, with the ultimate goal of restoring CFTR function. These particles could carry RNA strands encoding the missing protein, or gene-editing tools that fix the mutation directly.

This is a deeply personal essay about the last 30 years of cystic fibrosis research, the extraordinary difficulty of delivering gene therapies into the lungs, and what it’s like to try to cure your own disease. We’re extremely honored that Jacob decided to write this! The piece is charming and irreverent and, I think, a reflection of his personality.

https://t.co/pEws53LR5K

text:
Thoughts from my Shanghai field trip

Sentiment among Greater China investors was far worse than I expected. Unlike the US market, A shares had not seen a single rebound since July. Still holding Chinese and Hong Kong AI stocks that had crashed and Korean memory stocks that had collapsed, investors kept pressing me on when memory would bounce back.

Many investors said the AI trade was over, and a few said they doubted whether even 2027 capex, not just 2028, would go ahead as planned.

Overall, the bearish sentiment was so strong that even I, a bull before coming to China, started to waver.

It got to the point where, faced with the bear case that memory prices could start falling in the third quarter of next year, I took it seriously and couldn't refute it.

As the conversations went on, I gradually began to understand where their pessimism was coming from. In the end, they were all asking the same question.

So what comes after AI coding? What will be the next engine of ARR for Anthropic and OpenAI?

Several candidates came up. AI4S, AI chip design, and so on... But none of them clearly convinced investors.

I couldn't offer a clear answer either. Sure, there are rumors that Anthropic has made major breakthroughs in both AI4S and AI chip design, but what we actually want to know is when any of that turns into money.

With AI4S, there could be beneficiaries right away, such as companies that sell lab monkeys or diagnostic kits. In fact, there already are. But while we can trade those names in the short term, what we ultimately want to know is whether Anthropic can make money by developing drugs. That is still several years away.

As for AI chip design, the TAM itself is hard to calculate, and even if you do calculate it, it is hard to monetize. That makes it difficult for the market to believe in.

Honestly, this feels like the hardest market in history. If a company isn't making money, selling makes sense. But right now the market sells even when companies are making money, even when they beat, and even when they say demand will stay solid all the way through 2028 and 2029.

So my recommendation to investors was to buy memory, and within memory, DRAM. Not because I have conviction in the DRAM cycle, but because I see it as a relatively defensive choice within the AI trade.

Memory stocks are now trading close to 1x P/B on 2027 BPS. Historically, memory stocks have staged technical rebounds when they fell below 1x P/B.

And even if the broader market falls further from here, the three DRAM makers will keep buying back their own shares. I thought that would guarantee a certain level of buying and concluded the stocks would have downside support.

Of course, I don't know whether memory stocks can break above their previous highs. That depends on whether sentiment across the broader market recovers. But I think there is a fairly good chance that memory outperforms the rest of the AI trade.

text:
@VitalikButerin opened @EFDevcon with it: we need to be able to trust our operating systems and our hardware — a formally verified OS, open silicon.

Here is a piece of that, running today. Eita: an EVM specified in @leanprover Lean 4, with the code that runs emitted from the spec. Open source, MIT.

What it is
The EVM's semantics are a Lean 4 translation of the Ethereum execution specs (EELS), clause by clause, Frontier to Osaka, with Amsterdam staged, plus the OP Stack and Arc chain rules. The code that runs — the ARM64 and x86-64 interpreter handlers, JIT code, gas formulas, and the effect layer for calls, creates, storage and transaction application — is emitted from that spec, not written by hand; on ARM64 the handlers are proved against the spec at the instruction level. CI fails if the committed generated code differs from what the emitters produce. Not "audited": specified, derived, and checked.

Checked against the real chain, every block
It re-executes @ethereum mainnet and @circle's @arc mainnet from genesis and follows both live: gas used, logs bloom, receipts and transactions roots, EELS validate_header (base fee included) on every block, and the full state root every 10,000 blocks on Ethereum and at each 32,768-block anchor on Arc. That loop also caught our own mistakes: a missing P-256 precompile in our Base rules, and an SBCL 2.6.0 miscompile that corrupted wide integers in snapshot records.

What a replay sees that logs don't
• 2 Nov: 8 USDT destroyBlackFunds calls zeroed 2,529,259.73 USDT of blacklisted balances — a DestroyedBlackFunds event, no Transfer.
• 27 Oct–2 Nov: 41% of the ERC-20 holder-events we checked were Transfer logs from a token whose storage did not change in that transaction.
• One token credits balances in mint() and emits nothing: 23,614 silent balance changes in a week.
Live at https://t.co/NGDp98DyVw, with what is proved, what is checked and what is still trusted spelled out: https://t.co/j85QDqOQ5V

It's early. 19 proof obligations are still open and tracked in the repo. It isn't an execution client yet: an Engine API block source is the step that makes it one.

The next frontier: hardware
The techniques behind Eita — a Lean specification, the implementation derived from it, a continuous check against the real system — matter even more for secure hardware, where a bug is etched into silicon and can't be patched. Lean-specified firmware and RTL on open silicon is where "trust our hardware" gets real, and it's what I'm building now: https://t.co/gEe5ILT0QB (@beledgerless), together with @maqstik and @sbellem to the future of mobile trusted compute.

Credit where it's due: this work was motivated by conversations moths ago with @ilyasergey and his team at &Truth (@andTruthPBC), out of stealth last week. The more of us building this, the sooner verified code becomes the default.

I'll be at #Devcon in Mumbai Thursday to Saturday. Happy to talk. @ethereumfndn.

text:
Huge congrats to Succinct’s Rahul Dalal, one of the cryptographers behind FlashProve, @AnthropicAI’s provable inference system built on zkSNARKs.

Why: Today, AI runs on a “just trust me” model. Users can’t verify that a response came from the model they chose, or that an attacker didn’t tamper with it along the way. As AI takes on higher-stakes work, that create tension for users, labs, and regulators alike.

What: Researchers from Anthropic, EPFL, MIT, and @SuccinctLabs built FlashProve, a system that lets a model provider commit to a specific model and then prove each response was produced by it, without revealing the weights. Under the hood, it uses zkSNARKs, the same cryptographic technology Succinct uses to secure $13.5B in deposits on Ethereum L2s.

So What: FlashProve proved Llama 4 Maverick, a 400B-parameter LLM, at 110 tokens/sec on a single H100 GPU, with ~19 MB proofs. That puts proving at roughly 70 to 95x the cost of running the model. The previous standard for the same model was ~0.02 tokens/sec.

What’s Next: FlashProve is still a research prototype, but it’s a step change toward the question we asked with Flock earlier this year: how close can proving get to computing? The closer it gets, the less reason there is to release any output without a proof attached.

Congrats again to Rahul and the FlashProve team, and great to see @Starknet, @Mantle_Official (proven by Succinct), and several zkML projects cited.

quoted_text:
Most people are still using AI the wrong way.

They ask it questions.

Elon Musk just pointed at the right way.

Yesterday, Jason Ginsberg wrote: "Treat Grok Bot like a teammate and give @bot an ambitious task you'd normally give to a new hire."

Elon's answer: "This is the way."

Three words. A whole shift in how we work.

Here's what that looks like in real life.

Scott Billows runs a business with a very traditional sales cycle. Deals that take months to cultivate.

He pointed Grok Bot at his company's tools.

It dug through the past. Surfaced old prospects and customers nobody was calling anymore. Handed them to his sales reps.

Two weeks in, a closed deal.

His words: "Without Grok Bot we most likely would not have reached out to this past customer."

Think about that.

Not a faster search. Not a smarter autocomplete. Not a chatbot.

A teammate that found money hiding in plain sight.

Everyone thought AI would be a better answer machine.

It's actually a new kind of colleague.

Elon put it plainly back in October: "assume you are hiring a super competent employee."

Not a tool you open. Someone you hand the job to.

The team keeps adding powers. Product pages. Order tracking. Payments. Team Bots your whole company can share.

Every week the job description gets longer.

Here's the part almost nobody sees yet.

For all of history, having a team was a privilege. Only the rich, the big companies, the well-connected could delegate.

Everyone else did everything alone.

That wall is falling.

A small shop owner. A single parent. A sailor at sea. Anyone can now say: "Here's the mission. Go."

When everyone gets a team, everyone becomes a builder.

And a civilization of builders doesn't stay small for long.

Stop asking AI questions.

Give it a job.

Here's how to understand the CFTC equity perp news, simplified:

The @CFTC has approved equity perp contracts for the 4 exchanges that have filed requests to approve them:

- KalshiEX LLC
- Coinbase Derivatives
- Bitnomial (Kraken)
- Nadex/OG.com 

All 4 of these exchanges are:
1. CFTC registered exchanges
2. DCMs that clear trades with registered DCOs
3. Also registered with the SEC
4. That previously filed requests for approval of equity-perp contracts. 

The 4 exchanges have internal standards (which they've formalized and filed with the CFTC) for which equity-perp they can list on their own exchange. 

Things like 
- Equity is publicly traded
- Sufficient float, trading volume
- Reliable pricing to be able to calc funding payments
- Market structure resilient to manipulation

So the exchanges are *mostly* free to self-certify the markets they want, i.e. all the popular ones. Which is bullish, because we're about to get a lot of onshore equity perps available on US retail platforms like Coinbase, Kraken. 

btw, @Lighter_xyz will file with the @CFTC this month (per their Q3 investor call) and will very likely be the 5th exchange on this list (and the only crypto-native DEX with a CFTC DCM/DCO license), and is one of the reasons why Lighter is so unique as a project

text:
Sequoia Capital just hosted AI Ascent and gathered 150 of the top AI minds like Demis Hassabis, Andrej Karpathy, Greg Brockman, Boris Cherny of Anthropic 🤯

And Sequoia just gave one of the clearest frameworks for where AI is going.

The core idea:
- AI is not just another software wave.
- Cloud expanded the software market.
- AI expands the services market.

That means the next giant AI companies may not sell tools, dashboards, or copilots.

They may sell the work itself.

The full breakdown:

1/12. AI is the biggest platform shift yet
Cloud took software from roughly $350B to $650B.
AI opens something much larger:
A $10T+ services market that machines can now start to address.

2/12. This wave is moving faster than cloud or mobile
Every technology wave creates billion-dollar companies.
But AI companies are reaching massive scale much faster.
What took decades in cloud may take years in AI.

3/12. This is a computation revolution, not just a communication revolution
The internet changed how information was distributed.
AI changes how information is processed.
That is a much deeper shift.

4/12. We are moving from faster horses to cars
The first AI apps made workers 10–40% more productive.
Useful, but not transformational.
The next generation creates 10–40x improvements.

5/12. Sequoia’s practical definition of AGI is simple
Forget the philosophical debate.
If a system can be dispatched to do a job, recover from failure, and keep going until the task is complete…
For business purposes, that is what matters.

6/12. The race is now for the services economy
Software companies used to sell systems of record.
AI companies can now sell outcomes.
Not “here is software to help your lawyer.”

7/12. The best moat is not the model
In AI, the underlying technology changes too fast.
Today’s breakthrough becomes tomorrow’s baseline.
So the moat is not just technical capability.
The moat is customer intimacy.

8/12. Founders should wrap around customers, not model releases
Most technical founders want to chase the latest model.
But the model layer keeps shifting.

9/12. Affordance matters more than people think
Raw model power is not enough.
A terminal, API, or blank chat box may be powerful, but most users don’t know what to do with it.

10/12. The diffusion gap is the opportunity
Frontier models improve every week.
Enterprises absorb change over months or years.
That gap is massive.

11/12. 2026 is the year of agents
2022–2024 was chat.
2024–2025 was reasoning.
2026 is agents.

12/12. Services is the new software
AI is moving from helping humans do cognitive work…
to replacing entire categories of cognitive work.
Actual work, done end-to-end.

Full breakdown here: Sequoia AI Ascent 2026: The future of AI

author: zGuz
quoted_text:
Last night, my lawyers moved to sanction World Liberty Financial @worldlibertyfi for failing to disclose, until months into my litigation against the company, that it is a citizen of the UAE 🇦🇪 . #WLFI #USD1 

For those who are new to this dispute, I was one of World Liberty’s earliest and largest investors.  In November 2024, I agreed to buy $30 million of $WLFI tokens under a Token Purchase Agreement with World Liberty, and I later increased my total investment to $45 million. 

In April, I sued World Liberty, alleging that the company induced my investment through fraud and then unlawfully froze my tokens.

My Token Purchase Agreement gives me the right to bring my claims in either California federal or state court.  

I chose federal court.

Federal courts can hear a case like mine only when the two sides come from different places.  Foreign plaintiffs like me can sue an American defendant in federal court, but foreign plaintiffs generally cannot sue a foreign defendant there.  For these purposes, a company like World Liberty takes on the citizenship of each of its owners, so a single foreign owner makes the company foreign.  

In other words, so long as World Liberty and all of its owners were American, my case could be heard in federal court.

The federal court’s rules required World Liberty to file a disclosure at the start of the case identifying every one of its owners and where each is a citizen.  World Liberty’s disclosure identified only one entity—World Liberty itself—and listed Florida as its sole citizenship.  Its lawyers certified that they were unaware of anyone else who needed to be disclosed.

World Liberty then moved to compel arbitration, seeking to pull my case out of open court and into secret arbitration proceedings. 

I opposed that motion, and my lawyers spent months and hundreds of thousands of dollars fighting it.  At a hearing in August, the Court signaled that it was not persuaded that my claims belonged in arbitration.  Instead, the Court ruled that certain of my claims should stay in open court, and certain claims should be sent to arbitration, and ordered the parties to meet and confer to come up with a proposed agreement on which claims stay in open court and which ones go to arbitration.

Less than a week later, World Liberty suddenly “corrected” its disclosure.  Where it had previously listed only one member in its ownership chain, it now listed 22, and claimed citizenship in Florida, Delaware, Puerto Rico, and the UAE.  

World Liberty now says that the federal court has no jurisdiction over my case, since its UAE citizenship means there are foreign parties on both sides of the case.

The irony is hard to miss.  World Liberty’s gold paper declares that “[b]y design, World Liberty Financial is not organized offshore,” and that it is “an American, tax-paying, corporation that aims to bring DeFi to its rightful home—America.”  It promises a “US-based decentralized platform” built on “American ideals of liberty, privacy, and freedom to transact,” calls private, intermediary-free transactions “a core American value,” and boasts that “[r]ather than shying away from the United States, World Liberty Financial embraces the United States as the future CRYPTO CAPITAL OF THE PLANET.”

World Liberty was proudly American 🇺🇸 when it was selling tokens.  It discovered its UAE 🇦🇪 roots only when it needed a way out of an American federal courtroom.

World Liberty presumably always knew who its owners were.  Its lawyers claim that they learned about the company’s UAE citizenship only after they filed the original disclosure.  

As my motion explains, if that is true, then either World Liberty’s lawyers failed to conduct appropriate diligence, or World Liberty did not give its lawyers a straight answer.  When we asked how this happened, World Liberty refused to tell us.

Token holders deserve to know whether the projects they invest in are telling the truth, both to the public and to courts.  I am filing this motion to hold World Liberty and its lawyers accountable for what I believe was a misleading disclosure to the Court, and to make sure that the cost of World Liberty’s gamesmanship falls on them, not on me.  

And after my sanctions motion is resolved in federal court, I will re-file my lawsuit against World Liberty in California state court.

I will keep fighting for the transparency this community deserves.

text:
Anthropic's finances are deteriorating ahead of its IPO:

Anthropic reported +$16.96 billion in Q3 2026 revenue, up +47% QoQ.

However, quarterly revenue growth slowed sharply from +144% in Q2, as price reductions and contractual discounts offset revenue by ~$600 million.

Meanwhile, Anthropic's operating profitability lasted just ONE quarter as the company swung back to a GAAP operating loss of -$567 million in Q3, following operating income of +$974 million in Q2.

This comes as compute and infrastructure expenses surged +77% QoQ to $9.9 billion, accounting for 58% of revenue, up from 48% in Q2. 

In effect, every $1 spent on computing infrastructure generated just $1.72 in revenue, down from $2.08 in Q2, marking the first quarterly deterioration in this key efficiency metric.

Overall, Anthropic's net loss reached -$23.3 billion in Q3, bringing its cumulative net loss for the first 9 months of 2026 to a staggering -$104 billion.

While most of the quarterly net loss came from non-cash valuation adjustments, the underlying operating business also slipped back into the red.

Excluding the $21.9 billion in non-cash valuation adjustments, Anthropic's Q3 net loss was -$1.4 billion.

Anthropic's trillion-dollar AI ambitions are increasingly colliding with the financial reality of an infrastructure race where computing costs are rising faster than revenue.

author: YumaGroup
quoted_text:
fugal is live on bittensor: subnet 70.

the best model for your question often isn't the most expensive one. and which one is best keeps changing: new flagships, new prices, and nobody is paid to keep re-measuring.

fugal is an llm router. it reads your question, predicts which model will get it right, weighs that against price, and calls that one model. built to give you frontier answers at a fraction of the cost.

subnet 70 is how it stays right. miners compete to train better routers, every benchmark runs inside intel tdx so results can't be faked, and they only earn when their router beats every fixed choice of models at the same cost. so the only way to win is a router that gets more right for less.

author: frogmonkee
quoted_text:
Huge congrats to Succinct’s Rahul Dalal, one of the cryptographers behind FlashProve, @AnthropicAI’s provable inference system built on zkSNARKs.

Why: Today, AI runs on a “just trust me” model. Users can’t verify that a response came from the model they chose, or that an attacker didn’t tamper with it along the way. As AI takes on higher-stakes work, that create tension for users, labs, and regulators alike.

What: Researchers from Anthropic, EPFL, MIT, and @SuccinctLabs built FlashProve, a system that lets a model provider commit to a specific model and then prove each response was produced by it, without revealing the weights. Under the hood, it uses zkSNARKs, the same cryptographic technology Succinct uses to secure $13.5B in deposits on Ethereum L2s.

So What: FlashProve proved Llama 4 Maverick, a 400B-parameter LLM, at 110 tokens/sec on a single H100 GPU, with ~19 MB proofs. That puts proving at roughly 70 to 95x the cost of running the model. The previous standard for the same model was ~0.02 tokens/sec.

What’s Next: FlashProve is still a research prototype, but it’s a step change toward the question we asked with Flock earlier this year: how close can proving get to computing? The closer it gets, the less reason there is to release any output without a proof attached.

Congrats again to Rahul and the FlashProve team, and great to see @Starknet, @Mantle_Official (proven by Succinct), and several zkML projects cited.

text:
A dataset sample that looks perfect may be the least useful sample to buy from.

As a procurement lead, you need to discover the mismatch before you sign—not after you receive the files.

Ask for a representative sample that includes:
• Typical records, not just the cleanest examples
• The exact file and metadata schema
• Known exclusions and missing fields
• Annotation conventions, where applicable
• Licensing and permitted-use information

Then run one small ingestion or evaluation test against your real acceptance criteria.

If the supplier can only show a polished demo but cannot explain what it represents, you do not yet have enough evidence to judge fit.

AIxBlock offers off-the-shelf audio and custom data sourcing, collection, and annotation. The right route depends on your coverage, rights, and format needs.

Looking for data you can actually evaluate before procurement? Share the requirements with AIxBlock: https://t.co/V8BlCj2eLG

text:
Equity perpetuals are here: Americans can now trade perpetual futures on individual stocks listed on U.S. exchanges for the first time.

The @CFTC deemed the contracts approved as security futures, which the CFTC and @SECGov regulate jointly. U.S. investors get the protections of both agencies, the oversight Congress intended when it created a dedicated regime for security futures products.

In our August comment letter, we made the case that security futures treatment is the best path for these markets to flourish. Both CFTC- and SEC-regulated exchanges can list security futures, so venues primarily overseen by either agency can compete to offer this new class of product. That competition will improve outcomes for investors.

Equity perpetuals expand the tools that market participants can use to manage risk and take positions on securities in a single contract that never expires. We commend the staff of both agencies for this milestone in our derivatives markets.

text:
Aave 正在推动一件可能改变整个 DeFi 行业的事情。

11月3日，Aave Labs 联合 Kamino、Veda，公开了一份提交给美国 SEC 的法律框架。

核心诉求很有意思：
去中心化借贷协议，不应该被当作证券发行人或传统金融中介来监管。

而且，他们不是请求 SEC 给 DeFi 特殊豁免，而是认为按照现有证券法，符合条件的去中心化借贷本来就不应该属于证券交易。

几个核心观点：
1、用户把资产存入借贷市场，不等于把钱交给某家公司投资，也不存在传统意义上的收益承诺。
2、DAO 投票决定利率、抵押率、清算参数，是制定市场规则，不是替用户管理投资组合。
3、非托管 Vault 即使采用自动化策略，只要管理权限受到代码约束、用户保留资产权益，也不应该自动被认定为投资基金。
4、判断一项交易是否属于证券，应该看实际法律关系，而不是看有没有发行 Token。

小晖晖认为，这件事的意义可能比 Aave 本身大得多。

过去十几年，Crypto 一直在争论一个问题：

DeFi 究竟是金融产品，还是金融基础设施？

如果美国监管最终认可 Aave 提出的部分原则，那么去中心化借贷协议就有机会获得更清晰的法律地位。

这对 Aave、Morpho、Kamino，以及整个链上借贷和 RWA 抵押融资市场，都可能产生深远影响。

尤其是 RWA。

未来如果大量代币化股票、国债、基金份额进入链上市场，谁来提供抵押融资、流动性和自动清算？

小晖晖认为，Aave 这样的借贷协议，有机会成为链上资本市场的基础设施。

但还有一个问题不能回避：

Aave 协议的商业价值增长，究竟有多少能够传导到 AAVE 代币？

监管确定性可以改善估值预期，却不能自动创造代币价值。

真正需要观察的，还是借贷需求、协议净收入、回购，以及 AAVE 持有人的价值捕获。

从 Uniswap 到 Aave，小晖晖越来越坚定一个判断：

DeFi 下一轮最大的机会，可能不再是跟散户抢交易量，而是成为传统金融进入链上世界时绕不开的基础设施。

当然，目前这只是行业向 SEC 提交的法律主张，不代表 SEC 已经批准。

但方向值得持续关注。

未来十年，链上金融最大的公司，未必是最会讲故事的，而可能是那些真正承担金融市场底层功能的协议。

It's officially election day.

History says stocks are heading higher.

In fact, the S&P 500 has closed GREEN in the year following every US Midterm election since 1980.

As we noted in our analysis yesterday, we believe recent weakness in markets is largely a function of the uncertainty around Midterm elections.

However, when this uncertainty dissipates, markets react positively.

Since 1980, the S&P 500 has averaged a +14% gain in the 12 months following US Midterm elections.

Furthermore, even after divided-government outcomes, the index has averaged a +15% one-year gain, compared to +12% under single-party control.

Of course, the near-term picture will come with volatility and change.

But, if history is any guide, it's a great time to be bullish.

Turn on our post notifications at @KobeissiLetter for real-time analysis as this develops.

text:
Here's how to understand the CFTC equity perp news, simplified:

The @CFTC has approved equity perp contracts for the 4 exchanges that have filed requests to approve them:

- KalshiEX LLC
- Coinbase Derivatives
- Bitnomial (Kraken)
- Nadex/OG.com 

All 4 of these exchanges are:
1. CFTC registered exchanges
2. DCMs that clear trades with registered DCOs
3. Also registered with the SEC
4. That previously filed requests for approval of equity-perp contracts. 

The 4 exchanges have internal standards (which they've formalized and filed with the CFTC) for which equity-perp they can list on their own exchange. 

Things like 
- Equity is publicly traded
- Sufficient float, trading volume
- Reliable pricing to be able to calc funding payments
- Market structure resilient to manipulation

So the exchanges are *mostly* free to self-certify the markets they want, i.e. all the popular ones. Which is bullish, because we're about to get a lot of onshore equity perps available on US retail platforms like Coinbase, Kraken. 

btw, @Lighter_xyz will file with the @CFTC this month (per their Q3 investor call) and will very likely be the 5th exchange on this list (and the only crypto-native DEX with a CFTC DCM/DCO license), and is one of the reasons why Lighter is so unique as a project

text:
In this new formal verification challenge, both in Lean and Rocq, the aim is to make the fastest formally verified implementation of the EVM, the Ethereum Virtual Machine.

The verification is to be done at the assembly level in RISC-V, going through a verified compiler like CakeML, but this is only a suggestion. The initial target is to minimize the worst execution case by proving an upper bound on all possible inputs.

The EVM is composed of three parts: parsing, the execution itself in a stack-based machine, and the cryptographic primitives. The aim is to denial of services for future ZK versions of Etherum while optimizing the general process.

Formal verification enables extra secure development and optimizations, and can targets increasingly complex projects like this one.

The link to the challenge in the quoted tweet 👇
author: guillaumeclaret
quoted_text:
What's the most work that could possibly be required to verify an Ethereum block?

Today, we can't prove an answer. All we know is the validator always finishes. https://t.co/Y5w3tlKLCC is an open challenge to change that: contributors compete on a leaderboard to find mathematically guaranteed bounds for verifying Ethereum, no matter what's in a block.

Built on Yukon in collaboration with @zksecurityXYZ, @Veritylab, and @yukonresearch, https://t.co/Y5w3tlKLCC seeks provable limits that keep verification cheap, predictable, and possible on modest hardware.
