author: HarryStebbings
quoted_text:
The best question I ask every single person on 20VC is:

“What do you know now that you wish you had known 12 months ago?”

My answer: the demand for inference is infinite. It is truly so much larger than any of us comprehend.

It will be very hard for neo-cloud providers to move into this market effectively.

We will have 3-4 specialised inference providers worth $300-$500BN in this market.

@modal is one of them. $1BN in ARR. $300M in sandbox revenue alone. WTF.

Erik @bernhardsson is also one of the coolest, most authentic people I have had the fortune of having on the show. Money on cos he is European! 😉

We sat down to shoot the s*** and my notes below.

1. Why I Hate the Description of Entrepreneurship as Pain and Eating Glass. That Is BS

Erik rejects the idea that building a company means suffering pain for a big reward at the end. He enjoys work every day, even the hard conversations, and hopes to work on Modal for 20 to 50 years. He has no wish to sell, saying he "would just go and start Modal 2."

2. Why the Days of 90% Software Margins Are Totally Gone

Almost no company today has the 90%-plus software margins common in Silicon Valley a decade ago. A dollar paid at the top of the stack flows through applications, models, infrastructure, cloud and NVIDIA, with each layer taking 20% to 30% gross margins. Erik sees Modal reaching 40% to 60% margins long term, but never software margins.

Are the days of 90% margins over or is this just the buildout phase of the new cycle meaning margin reduction @venkyganesan @AnjneyMidha

3. Why Inference Alone Will Become Commoditized, and You Have to Have a Suite of Products Around It

Selling inference alone is a commodity business with no switching costs and a race to the bottom. Erik argues it must come with post-training, sandboxes, agentic tooling, reinforcement learning, and low-latency and batch inference. Modal has spent five years building that infrastructure, which he calls very hard to copy.

Do you agree, inference will be commoditised and product breadth is the secret to retention @evishria @sarahcat21

4. Why We Will Have More Not Fewer Engineers in the Future

Every time programmers become more efficient, demand for software rises. Erik says the job was never translating English into code but understanding human requirements, and that work keeps moving up the stack, from assembly and punch cards to Python and now agents. He expects software engineers to be fine for the next 10 to 20 years.

What does no one see that everyone should see about the future of software engineering @matansf @pmarca @rabois

5. The Wildest Prediction on the Future of the Inference Market

The inference market has grown 10x to 100x bigger than Erik expected, and he predicts it will split into many specialized segments. He sees room for low-latency, high-latency, fine-tuning and post-training offerings, plus new hardware and technologies that need far fewer resources.

What is your wildest prediction on the future of the inference market @gavinsbaker @eladgil @romanchernin

6. The $15.75 Billion Company That Has Never Made a Pitch Deck

Modal has never made a pitch deck for any of its rounds. Erik gets to know investors well before raising and had spoken with Rich and Gonzalo at Accel for at least a year before the D round, so the deal came together very quickly.

At the keynote of Unreal Fest Tokyo 2026 (November 3–4, 2026, Tokyo), Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney announced significant changes for Unreal Engine 6 (UE6):

Blueprints (BP) and Actors will be removed (not merely deprecated) in UE6.

This is a shift from the earlier plan announced at Unreal Fest Chicago / State of Unreal in June 2026, where they were expected to remain in early versions and later be deprecated.⁠

The C++ Gameplay Framework will also be abolished. Game logic will fully migrate to Verse + Scene Graph.
C++ will continue to be used for core engine systems (rendering, physics, etc.), but not for the gameplay framework.⁠

Reasons given: higher development productivity, better content portability/interoperability across games and ecosystems, and stronger compatibility with AI-assisted development. 

Epic reported significant efficiency gains from internal Verse-based work.⁠

Tim Sweeney acknowledged it as a “painful change” and apologized to developers attached to Blueprints. He noted that Epic itself is experiencing the same pain (e.g., migrating Fortnite to Verse without service interruption).

Migration support: AI-powered conversion tools are planned to help transition from Blueprints/C++ to Verse (exact form TBD).

Projects already in development on UE5 can continue on the UE5 branch (including UE5.9 and future 5.x releases).⁠

UE6 Early Access remains targeted for the end of 2027.
The event also features 30+ sessions covering games (Sega, ACE COMBAT 8, etc.), film, architecture, automotive, digital twins, UEFN, MetaHuman, and deep dives into Verse/Scene Graph.

Bottom line: UE6 is moving to a Verse-centric programming model and will remove the traditional Actor / Blueprint / C++ Gameplay Framework.

So, What do you thinks about these changes?

text:
So Anthropic has a paper on SNARKs for proving the correctness of LLM inference. The idea of snarks for LLMs is that you can check a response came from the claimed model without the operator exposing the model’s weights.

It's Cool work. TL;DR: it’s about 70-95x slower than their chosen baseline, which is very impressive.

I’m still reading, but my biggest question is whether that overhead is really ~100x. if I spent a few million tokens’ worth of engineering effort, would the baseline improve more than their SNARK scheme?

Of course, at some point this doesn’t matter. The point is cost for the capability. If you want verifiable LLM results, on a non-local model, and can’t use a TEE, is 100x overhead acceptable?

Note: they do this with a mixture-of-experts model and prove after the fact, in batches, so the prover only does work for the experts that actually ran. That doesn’t seem to translate to 100 tokens/second for other models. But like I said, I’m still reading.

For anyone else reading along: yeah, prices are down, we all see the chart, but this FUD isn't even trying.

1. We increased emissions to SOAP Bitcoin. 

To pull SHA-256 and Scrypt hashrate away from legacy chains, you have to pay miners to point their machines at Quai.

SOAP has already burned over 233M QUAI, wiping out the majority of daily mining emissions and bringing net mining inflation down to around 4.7% a year.

 After Polaris and SOAP burns, Quai's total inflation is single-digit (~8.7%) with nearly 93% of the supply already circulating.

Last night, my lawyers moved to sanction World Liberty Financial @worldlibertyfi for failing to disclose, until months into my litigation against the company, that it is a citizen of the UAE 🇦🇪 . #WLFI #USD1 

For those who are new to this dispute, I was one of World Liberty’s earliest and largest investors.  In November 2024, I agreed to buy $30 million of $WLFI tokens under a Token Purchase Agreement with World Liberty, and I later increased my total investment to $45 million. 

In April, I sued World Liberty, alleging that the company induced my investment through fraud and then unlawfully froze my tokens.

My Token Purchase Agreement gives me the right to bring my claims in either California federal or state court.  

I chose federal court.

Federal courts can hear a case like mine only when the two sides come from different places.  Foreign plaintiffs like me can sue an American defendant in federal court, but foreign plaintiffs generally cannot sue a foreign defendant there.  For these purposes, a company like World Liberty takes on the citizenship of each of its owners, so a single foreign owner makes the company foreign.  

In other words, so long as World Liberty and all of its owners were American, my case could be heard in federal court.

The federal court’s rules required World Liberty to file a disclosure at the start of the case identifying every one of its owners and where each is a citizen.  World Liberty’s disclosure identified only one entity—World Liberty itself—and listed Florida as its sole citizenship.  Its lawyers certified that they were unaware of anyone else who needed to be disclosed.

World Liberty then moved to compel arbitration, seeking to pull my case out of open court and into secret arbitration proceedings. 

I opposed that motion, and my lawyers spent months and hundreds of thousands of dollars fighting it.  At a hearing in August, the Court signaled that it was not persuaded that my claims belonged in arbitration.  Instead, the Court ruled that certain of my claims should stay in open court, and certain claims should be sent to arbitration, and ordered the parties to meet and confer to come up with a proposed agreement on which claims stay in open court and which ones go to arbitration.

Less than a week later, World Liberty suddenly “corrected” its disclosure.  Where it had previously listed only one member in its ownership chain, it now listed 22, and claimed citizenship in Florida, Delaware, Puerto Rico, and the UAE.  

World Liberty now says that the federal court has no jurisdiction over my case, since its UAE citizenship means there are foreign parties on both sides of the case.

The irony is hard to miss.  World Liberty’s gold paper declares that “[b]y design, World Liberty Financial is not organized offshore,” and that it is “an American, tax-paying, corporation that aims to bring DeFi to its rightful home—America.”  It promises a “US-based decentralized platform” built on “American ideals of liberty, privacy, and freedom to transact,” calls private, intermediary-free transactions “a core American value,” and boasts that “[r]ather than shying away from the United States, World Liberty Financial embraces the United States as the future CRYPTO CAPITAL OF THE PLANET.”

World Liberty was proudly American 🇺🇸 when it was selling tokens.  It discovered its UAE 🇦🇪 roots only when it needed a way out of an American federal courtroom.

World Liberty presumably always knew who its owners were.  Its lawyers claim that they learned about the company’s UAE citizenship only after they filed the original disclosure.  

As my motion explains, if that is true, then either World Liberty’s lawyers failed to conduct appropriate diligence, or World Liberty did not give its lawyers a straight answer.  When we asked how this happened, World Liberty refused to tell us.

Token holders deserve to know whether the projects they invest in are telling the truth, both to the public and to courts.  I am filing this motion to hold World Liberty and its lawyers accountable for what I believe was a misleading disclosure to the Court, and to make sure that the cost of World Liberty’s gamesmanship falls on them, not on me.  

And after my sanctions motion is resolved in federal court, I will re-file my lawsuit against World Liberty in California state court.

I will keep fighting for the transparency this community deserves.

text:
Prediction markets had Trump as a clear favourite in 2024 while the forecasters called it a coin flip. The markets were right.

Will they be right again tonight?

About $59M a day now rides on the midterms. So at @a1research__ we (and our agentic intern army) built three models and priced every liquid market on Polymarket and Kalshi against them.

What we found:

On who wins the House and the Senate, the market is right. Our models land within a few cents of the price and there's no arb left on the board.

Underneath, it contradicts itself tho. Nine contracts are priced 2 to 11 cents away from the markets they're built from. And five of those nine only pay out if the polls are overstating Democrats again. Same bet, five markets.

And on election night it has a blind spot you can use.

Every state counts its votes in a fixed order. Mail ballots first in some states, election day votes first in others, big cities last. So the running total leans one way for hours, and the direction is known before the first vote is in.

The market ignores that and prices whatever number is on the screen.

Michigan 2024. At 02:15 at night Rogers (R) was up 4.8 with 70% counted and Polymarket had him at 93.5c. Detroit hadn't reported yet. Slotkin (D) won by 0.3.

A model that knows Michigan's counting order, fed the same numbers at the same minute, had Rogers at 30c.

Tonight the same states count in the same order. The clock below tells you when each count can be trusted and which way the first number lies. Full model and the nine mispriced contracts in the article.

NFA tho. DYOR.

刚看到币安官推发布了安全调查报告，看完让人后背发凉，我根据我的理解梳理一下

9 月份：软件工程师 B 在一个正规的求职平台上，被一个「项目总监」联系，主动挖他。我猜大概率就是 LinkedIn 了，暴露了 B 是币安在职员工。

项目总监安排了两轮面试：一面是所谓 HR 视频面试，取得 B 的信任；二面是虚构公司的 CEO，通过 IM 进行，并且让 B 下载了一个包含恶意代码库的「作业」到他的工作电脑上。这个代码库的恶意代码，在安装过程中就执行了，引发了一系列未经授权的活动。而且这是一个 0-day 恶意软件，当时币安的终端安全软件都没检测出来，黑客还刻意清除了入侵痕迹，加大了发现和调查的难度。

10 月 20 号：黑客从 B 的电脑出发，借助币安公司内部的 AI 工具，控制了钱包运维工程师 A 和钱包软件工程师 C 的电脑。

控制 A 的电脑之后，黑客在上面发现了容器部署权限令牌。

10 月 29 日：黑客登录员工 C 的电脑，用从 A 那里偷来的凭证部署容器、运行恶意脚本，从而拿到内部钱包签名服务的访问权，在正常提现流程之外发起了转账。之后黑客又利用 EIP-7702 授权，批量转走了 ETH 链上的资产。

更早之前 6 月份的时候，A 其实在搜索引擎上搜热门 AI 编程工具后，就下载了被篡改的 Homebrew 安装包，但这次事件被安全团队及时发现了，没有酿成大祸。但工程师 A 的岗位及其钱包基础设施团队的相关同事，当时就已暴露给黑客

总结来说，这是一场多阶段攻击：结合了假面试、恶意软件下载、内部 AI 工具被利用、终端设备被入侵，以及高级的交易授权手法。

LinkedIn 暴露币安员工身份只是表象；A 下载被篡改的工具，让黑客锁定了钱包团队 + B 在工作电脑上运行「面试作业」直接打开大门，这才是根源；内部 AI 工具成了横向渗透的跳板，让黑客从一台电脑扩散到三个核心钱包工程师；而 EIP-7702 授权加上 MPC 钱包难以快速撤销，让事件在近 4 小时内没被完全控住，是催化剂

text:
A story about how Jane Street unwittingly reinvented datacenters in 2012, involving office server rooms, natural disasters, market maker obligations, recovery sites, colocation facilities, and old limestone telco buildings in lower Manhattan.

When I joined Jane Street from college in 2010, all of the firm’s proprietary trading systems ran out of a 8’X12’ server room on the 33rd floor of 1 New York Plaza, on the southern tip of Manhattan. Jane Street’s ETF market-making, options vol pricing, intercountry ADR arbitrage, and pan-equity stat-arb operated from this small deployment. The room itself was an engineering feat: the Dell server arrays were too heavy for the 1960s building’s floors to support, so the racks were affixed to the ceiling with concrete.

By 2012 Jane Street was not yet a member of most major US exchanges, even NYSE, and had virtually no presence in colocation facilities. Nevertheless, it was a ~$2B company experiencing rapid growth, a designated liquidity provider in most listed ETFs, a significant percentage of US and international equity volume, and a critical operator in capital markets.

In October 2012, Hurricane Sandy devastated lower Manhattan. 1 New York Plaza, Jane Street’s home, flooded to street level and the basement power generators were fully submerged. The resulting gas leaks made the office building hazardous to enter, and power and water were weeks away from being restored. Unprecedentedly, all major US exchanges closed for two business days after the storm but would be back up by day three. Jane Street was in danger of failing its lead-market-maker obligations if it didn’t relocate its business in time.

Jane Street had recently set up a partial office in a central New Jersey office park to comply with FINRA/SEC regulatory obligations for business continuity planning. A few engineers and I showed up to the empty site during the hurricane to begin mass-redeploying the firm’s software and infrastructure for the next critical 48 hours. A truckload of Dell PowerEdge R610s arrived the next morning, some salvaged from 1 New York Plaza’s server room, carried down 33 floors in pitch black by Jane Street’s IT team. For the next few months, everyone at the company from Rob Granieri to new-hires rode rented regional travel buses from Manhattan to NJ to keep Jane Street alive and growing.

When we all returned to Jane Street’s repaired 1 New York Plaza office in January 2013, the technology team realized something that’s obvious now: hardware doesn’t need to be colocated with people. The NJ disaster site had accidentally become Jane Street’s first firm-wide datacenter. The site afforded significantly more space, cheaper electricity, ground-floor weight support, and abundant cooling. This decision, to leave Jane Street’s servers in post-hurricane locations, would have profound effects on the firm’s infrastructure footprint and growth.

In 2013 it became a top priority for the technology and infrastructure teams to move all latency-sensitive trading into colocation facilities in order to cross-connect directly to exchange matching engine switches. And the search began for a new primary datacenter to house the firm’s research cluster and non-latency-sensitive applications.

In 2015 Jane Street found its new electronic home: lower Manhattan, limestone and 32-story windows, originally owned by the New York Telephone Company. It had retina-scan security and neon-colored liquid cooling and everything else we know today. They joined other major financial firms and software companies who had operated there for years.

In modeling disaster scenarios, experts tend to underrate the technological redundancies that already exist, or can be willed into rapid deployment, to ensure the US financial system remains secure.

text:
Really happy to see the response to the Darkbloom update :)

A few people asked: “Won’t the new sandbox providers just undercut you?”

The simple answer: we’re giving your agents a Mac.

We aren’t stopping at 2-4 vCPUs. We want to offer 8, 16 or 32 physical CPU cores, plus Apple GPUs, for agents doing research and complex work.

Unlike inference alone, these workloads can put much more of the machine to use. We think there’s a real opportunity to compete on both price and performance here.

My bet is that the work we give agents will keep getting more compute-intensive. Bigger builds, more experiments, simulations, video editing, rendering. There’s a lot beyond running a few commands and managing your calendar in a terminal.

Think about an agent working in Premiere Pro or Final Cut Pro, or using open-source creative tools. It needs access to the software, the environment and enough compute to actually do the work.

That’s what gets me excited about this. I want to see what agents can do when we give them a powerful Mac to work with.

That’s what we’re building towards with Darkbloom Sandboxes.

Cheers to the GOAT who made these chips! ❤️
author: gajesh
quoted_text:
Darkbloom just passed 1 trillion tokens processed :)

I haven't tweeted much recently or shared many charts. We've been heads down on the thing that matters most right now: getting providers more work and better earnings.

Honestly, it's been a hard stretch. Provider earnings have been low. People trusted us with their machines and their time, and we take that seriously.

Inference keeps getting cheaper as architectures improve and more supply comes online. That means more people can use AI, but it also makes the economics harder for our providers. We have to keep finding where these machines can be most useful.

The mission is still the same: bring together all the spare compute out there and make it easy to own & share AI. I believe in that more than when we started.

And there's a lot more these machines can do.

More agents means more code to run, more tests, more builds. All those actions need compute too. Apple has built some incredibly capable, energy-efficient CPUs, and we want to put them to work.

We've started the private beta for Darkbloom Sandboxes and CI/CD.

We're starting with our own pipelines, cutting our internal costs by 50% while leaving healthy margins for providers. This gives us another way to bring useful, paying work to the network.

If you're looking for Mac CI or sandboxes, let us know. We'd love to work with you.

We're also continuing to push on inference. There's a lot of work going into open-source clustering on top of MLX; huge kudos to @Spangler3000 and @TheDavidTai for absolutely killing it on that front and writing SOTA for  models such as GLM 5.3 Flash.

I'm attaching the debrief @0xkydo shared with providers last week. He laid out the difficult parts openly, and how people responded meant a lot to me. Seeing people care this much about making it work, especially through a hard stretch, reminds me why I love building this.

It's a hard problem. We're going to keep attacking it. Thank you to everyone who have been here in this journey and continuing to support & be with us.

text:
Garry Tan reveals why Y Combinator decides in just 10 minutes whether or not to fund a founder 

"The wild thing about Y Combinator is that we get 80,000, maybe 90,000 applications a year now for about 800 spots. So it is less than a 1% acceptance rate. Maybe 8 to 10% of those people would get an interview, sometimes less now." 

"And the wild thing is we actually spend only 10 minutes with them for that final stage."

"Paul Graham, the founder of YC, figured out that you didn't need half an hour, you don't need an hour. And then you could probably actually do it in about 5 minutes, but 5 minutes feels rude. So that's how YC ended up at 10 minutes."

"It sounds almost too simple, but 10 minutes is a wonderful constraint. Like how 140 characters for Twitter way back in the day was a wonderful constraint. If you can say something very simply that hits us, here's a user, here's a real person who has a problem, and here's how the technology that we build actually solves that. We just want to know what it is and why it's awesome."

"And then if we have a little bit of extra time, we want to know why that founder is the person to go and build that thing. And you can do all of that in 10 minutes. And it's an up-down decision." 

"Something like 10% to 15% of all self-made billionaires as of now, aged 50 and under, are YC alums."

Walter Isaacson: "Let's say Elon Musk, he walked in and you had 10 minutes with him. What do you think the percentage chance is that you would actually fund him?"

Garry Tan: "100%. In current form, 100%. I had a managing partner meeting the other day, and that's actually one of the example questions we ask ourselves to figure out whether we're on the right track." 

"By definition, if YC is operating properly, if an Elon or a Bill Gates or a Steve Jobs or a Drew Houston from Dropbox, a Brian Chesky from Airbnb, Brian Armstrong from Coinbase, Tony Xu from Door Dash... if someone like that walks into our office, can we say yes to them in 10 minutes? quoted_text:
Big news from @AnthropicAI  on verifiable LLM inference, with an exciting connection to Pearl’s proof of useful work.

Two orthogonal questions:
• Did the model you paid for actually produce this response?
• Was computational work performed?

Anthropic reports that generating inference proofs currently takes ~70–95× the GPU time of ordinary inference. Pearl’s PoUW, on the contrary, adds negligible overhead. These costs buy different guarantees. Proving correct inference doesn’t automatically establish proof of work and the other way around. But the two are deeply complementary. Verifiable inference could certify which model produced an answer, while Pearl׳s PoUW only certifies that a computation has been done.

As inference proofs get more practical, that combination could make AI easier to trust and more economical to provide.

Quite frankly I think what we're seeing with software hacks and this AirBnB stuff is just the simple societal rule that every rule in society exists because of the bottom quintile

A small percentage of bad actors use AI much faster than good actors can catch up - and now airlines, fridges, electronics, databases and god knows how many old companies w outdated infra are just getting hacked

I feel like we're witnessing the collapse of software from a cultural perspective. I don't know about software stocks, but I can feel that people at the fringes just hate using software

The solution isn't "use AI to fight the AI hacks" because that doesn't take into account the fabric of human nature - the solution that people will opt for is instead a mass exodus out of software

Unironically the only thing AI might have killed is the very thing that built it. We're basically reverting back to 2010s era type of stuff - IRL meetups, only booking hotels, etc. 

I think the conclusion of "oh but better software will be built" is just not intuitive because there are just a myriad of vectors beyond traditional software - like look at Binance social engineering hack. It was, at the end of the day, not a cyber-hack but a social engineering that could have only been done at scale using AI - imagine just some guy deploying 100 agents of a female and it's just a numbers game before one gets hit

It is what it is.

text:
Equity perpetuals are here: Americans can now trade perpetual futures on individual stocks listed on U.S. exchanges for the first time.

The @CFTC deemed the contracts approved as security futures, which the CFTC and @SECGov regulate jointly. U.S. investors get the protections of both agencies, the oversight Congress intended when it created a dedicated regime for security futures products.

In our August comment letter, we made the case that security futures treatment is the best path for these markets to flourish. Both CFTC- and SEC-regulated exchanges can list security futures, so venues primarily overseen by either agency can compete to offer this new class of product. That competition will improve outcomes for investors.

Equity perpetuals expand the tools that market participants can use to manage risk and take positions on securities in a single contract that never expires. We commend the staff of both agencies for this milestone in our derivatives markets.

总结下。

/ 我们将进入“新美元”时代
智能越充裕，对美元的需求就越高。
AI 模型让更多人、更多经济活动上线，人们未必能在美国开银行账户，却可以通过稳定币间接持有美债敞口。
消息应用 + 稳定币会作为分发网络，将美元分发到全球。

美国会赢；美元通道所有者也会赢。

/ 去寻找“传导手段”
技术起点不捕获大部分财富，财富落在拥有“传导手段”的人手里。
印刷术时代，古腾堡发明印刷却破产，财富被出版、发行与内容分发网络瓜分；
互联网时代，谷歌靠广告网络收取了大部分价值。

发明层吃糠，传导层抽租。
这个规律不会在 AI 时代被打破。

/ 去买还没被当成制高点定价的东西
千万不要做的:
只抱着上一代复合器（旧媒体、旧收费站）；
只买 AI 篮子当安全感；
指望卖前沿模型本身拿持久厚利。

智能会越来越强越来越便宜，要追逐的是尚未被定价，但会在未来规定智能如何变成经济活动的关卡与高地。

Security takeaways from the Binance hack, send this to your devs:

Never download or install apps/packages on MacOS without triple-checking the source first. Install homebrew from the developer's official page (https://t.co/Xt6KbK7weu) not from Google.

Job Interviews (one of the most common ways to hack lately):

1. Never do a job interview on your work laptop (obvious reasons)
2. Don't download software for the meeting (didn't happen here, but worth a mention)
3. If you have to clone a code repository and run its build/tests/scripts - it MUST be in a sandbox environment, never your machine

Simple, stupid, boring security practices, that can save billions when followed. Stay safe🙏

text:
Maybe I was a bit jaded about it all when I wrote my last post but going through the details of these hacks esp Binance, the attacks are only going to get more vicious and everyone needs to stay hyper paranoid across all attack vectors e.g social engineering, compromised device, exchange infra to smart contracts

And this is going to be the start of a new trend for L1s and onchain that want to bring on the masses, where consumer protection, security and regulation become a top prio

companies like Stripe, Coinbase, DRW etc that have distribution and touch the end user will push for more security, compliance, recovery and programmable controls at the protocol, token and wallet level. They have the biggest incentive to protect their users.

We're already seeing versions of this with Tempo building compliance and transfer controls into its infra, Canton with privacy and permissions for institutions, and Solana with Token Extensions that support freezing assets, transfer restrictions etc.

I believe precompiles and protocol level upgrades will play a much bigger role in the future of consumer adoption. And those with large distribution like Stripe, Coinbase, Robinhood  etc will push for these protections against malicious actors while onboarding millions of consumers and businesses onchain.

I've always thought onchain will split into two worlds. One where the masses will be, with financial products that have consumer protections, compliance, recovery etc and another thats purely permissionless, decentralized and largely the wild wild west.

Also specialized appchains like Hyperliquid have an advantage here. By building most of their infra in house around one product they can reduce some of the attack surfaces vs stitching together multiple protocols. And you could already see regulated players building compliant versions of HIP3 / HIP4 markets

Eventually  anyone that wants to tap into a global audience will have to follow regs in the markets they serve. And no, doesn’t mean the underlying chain has to be centralized either.

Which leaves another q what happens to the speculative liquidity on current chains today? If trillions in stablecoins, tokenized assets move onchain through companies with distribution, where does the speculative liquidity end up?

Eitherway I think the next onchain wars will be about who owns distribution, can capture/retain liquidity and who can protect the end user.

text:
Andrew Huberman on the best advice he ever got: figure out the most real work you can do every day, consistently, and find a way to reset every week.

"The best advice I ever got: there was a neurologist out at UC Berkeley and UCSF, Bob Knight, some years ago, very talented. I asked him for advice starting graduate school."

"He said, 'Figure out the maximum amount of real work that you can do every day consistently, and then figure out some non-destructive way to reset yourself every single week.'"

"I said, 'How do you reset?' He said he likes fishing. I like to hike. I like to get into nature and spend time with people while I do it. I figured out I could work X number of hours per day, 5 days a week, and I just stuck to it for 25 years."

"People who take a ton of stimulants and just blitz, blitz, blitz, blitz, blitz. These are the same people that crash and disappear. You have to figure out and build your capacity."

"Yes, you have to work extremely hard. You have to be extremely focused. But you also have to figure out how long you can keep this up."

quoted_text:
11/2 Marvell 为什么要买 Lumentum？Lumentum 增长这么快，为什么愿意卖？我希望这个帖子能够讲清楚，让你看明白这次 deal

All Stock Deal，光 x 半导体融合，这个可能是很多人一生一次的机会。

两者到的究竟是技术壁垒，还是暂时缺货的商品？ $MRVL $LITE

1/ Marvell CEO Matt Murphy：为什么收购，以及买到了什么技术壁垒
Marvell 的优势是 AI 互联所需的半导体技术，Lumentum 的优势是 AI 数据中心互联所需的光技术。两家公司结合，是为了打造 AI 互联领域的龙头。

背后的趋势是：光技术正在更深入地进入数据中心。当计算系统需要通过 scale-up 互联，把成百上千颗 GPU 连接起来时，就需要半导体和光技术无缝协同。他认为，这种融合将催生一种新的公司形态。

很多股东有担忧：Lumentum 的产品究竟具有技术差异化，还是只是暂时供不应求的标准化商品？如果交易完成需要超过 18 个月，到时短缺可能已经结束。

Matt 的回应主要有四点：
① 磷化铟和激光器技术具有很强的差异化。他认为，Lumentum 的光源、激光器与 Marvell 自有半导体技术结合后，能够形成客户黏性很强的解决方案。

② 目前售罄是因为需求快速增长。他表示，短期内看不到这种需求趋势改变；即使未来供需恢复平衡，这些产品的技术差异化仍会持续存在。他还提到，当前短缺遍及全球半导体与光行业，激光器只是其中一环。

③ 特殊工艺需要长期积累。他以自己在 Maxim 工作 22 年的经历作类比：BiCMOS、双极型、硅锗等技术涉及复杂的专有制造工艺，需要专业人才开发，不能简单等同于常规 CMOS 制造。他说，当时这些工艺由他们自行制造，并用“black magic”来形容其中很深、很专门的工艺诀窍。

④ 双方能够交叉验证需求。两家公司的产品进入相同的系统和设计项目，因此 Marvell 能用自身看到的需求核对 Lumentum 的增长情况。这让他们对其增长更有信心，也认为合并后能帮助客户更快推出产品。

2/ Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston：业绩这么好，为什么现在出售
他表示，公司刚公布的季度业绩可能是有史以来最好的几次表现之一，增长非常强劲。他提到该季度有 3.5 亿美元的增量增长；毛利率如今达到 53%，是公司见过的最好水平。

至于为什么选择现在交易，他的回答是：他们认为，行业融合的时机已经到了。

他提到 Marvell 此前收购 Inphi，认为 Matt 当时提前看到了光技术的发展趋势。现在，他们又看到了类似的转折点：半导体与光技术正在融合。

Michael 表示，如果不能率先行动，就可能落后。因此，Lumentum 希望迅速、果断地推进交易，推动 Matt 所说的这类新公司形成

text:
The bottleneck verifiable AI inference will hit:

A proof of inference only shows that the model ran correctly. The user supplies the input, so a forged input still yields a valid proof. Verifying the input is authentic is the bottleneck.

@AnthropicAI released FlashProve yesterday: a zkSNARK that an output came from a committed set of model weights. The user still checks only that their provider ran the right model. The moment the proof is shown to a third party as evidence, it is only as good as the input, and the proof says nothing about where the input came from.

Verifiable compute moves the trust from the party running the model to the party supplying the data.

That is why these proofs worked on blockchains first. A rollup's inputs are posted to the L1, so the proof covers data anyone can check. Off chain, there is a chronic shortage of verifiable data. A bank balance, a payroll record, a cap table or a lab result sits on a server that shows it to you over an encrypted connection. Once it leaves that server, it becomes a screenshot or a PDF.

Until the input carries provenance of its source, verifiable inference use cases will be limited. Verifiable data comes first. Verifiable compute is what you do with it.

“工程师 A 的电脑上存有一个具有生产环境容器部署权限的 Token”，这本身就是一个比较严重的凭证管理问题。对于这类高权限 Token，至少要坚持两个关键原则：

第一，内部自行生成的 Token，必须采用统一、易于识别的前缀。

例如通过公司或系统标识、环境标识，形成类似 sk_company_prod_xxxxxx 的固定前缀，便于扫描工具准确识别。

扫描范围也不能只覆盖代码仓库，还应包括工程师本地及 Home 目录下的隐藏文件、缓存、Session 文件和日志等，及时发现凭证被意外保存或泄露的位置。如果 Token 只是没有明显特征的随机字符串，扫描往往只能依赖格式和熵值判断，误报、漏报以及排查成本都会更高。

第二，能够直接操作生产环境的 Token，必须限制使用来源。

必须配置 IP 白名单或等效的网络访问限制，只允许通过公司 VPN 出口、指定跳板机或受控开发环境访问生产系统。即使 Token 被复制或泄露，也不应允许持有者从任意网络直接调用。

如果拿到一个 Token，就能在任何电脑、任何网络环境下操作生产系统，就意味着生产权限的安全几乎完全依赖这串凭证不被泄露，这是非常可怕的事情。

text:
Big news from @AnthropicAI  on verifiable LLM inference, with an exciting connection to Pearl’s proof of useful work.

Two orthogonal questions:
• Did the model you paid for actually produce this response?
• Was computational work performed?

Anthropic reports that generating inference proofs currently takes ~70–95× the GPU time of ordinary inference. Pearl’s PoUW, on the contrary, adds negligible overhead. These costs buy different guarantees. Proving correct inference doesn’t automatically establish proof of work and the other way around. But the two are deeply complementary. Verifiable inference could certify which model produced an answer, while Pearl׳s PoUW only certifies that a computation has been done.

As inference proofs get more practical, that combination could make AI easier to trust and more economical to provide.

text:
Peter Thiel's critique of European tech is sharper than most people quote it:

"In the social democratic European societies, it's acceptable to be moderately successful. It's not acceptable to be wildly successful."

That's not a cultural observation. It's a structural diagnosis.

Look at the pattern: Skype sold to Microsoft. Spotify relocated to New York and listed in the US. DeepMind sold to Google before it could compound. Klarna — one of Europe's most valuable fintechs — spent years being investigated and regulated the moment it hit scale.

The moment a European startup gets big enough to matter, the social contract shifts. Regulators, press, and public sentiment move from neutral to hostile. So founders learn to exit early — not because they lack ambition, but because the system taxes it.

Europe produces world-class talent and early-stage innovation. It just doesn't retain the compounding.

The constraint isn't capital. It's the ceiling culture places on acceptable ambition — and founders respond rationally to the incentives they're actually given.

text:
Garry Tan reveals why Y Combinator decides in just 10 minutes whether or not to fund a founder 

"The wild thing about Y Combinator is that we get 80,000, maybe 90,000 applications a year now for about 800 spots. So it is less than a 1% acceptance rate. Maybe 8 to 10% of those people would get an interview, sometimes less now." 

"And the wild thing is we actually spend only 10 minutes with them for that final stage."

"Paul Graham, the founder of YC, figured out that you didn't need half an hour, you don't need an hour. And then you could probably actually do it in about 5 minutes, but 5 minutes feels rude. So that's how YC ended up at 10 minutes."

"It sounds almost too simple, but 10 minutes is a wonderful constraint. Like how 140 characters for Twitter way back in the day was a wonderful constraint. If you can say something very simply that hits us, here's a user, here's a real person who has a problem, and here's how the technology that we build actually solves that. We just want to know what it is and why it's awesome."

"And then if we have a little bit of extra time, we want to know why that founder is the person to go and build that thing. And you can do all of that in 10 minutes. And it's an up-down decision." 

"Something like 10% to 15% of all self-made billionaires as of now, aged 50 and under, are YC alums."

Walter Isaacson: "Let's say Elon Musk, he walked in and you had 10 minutes with him. What do you think the percentage chance is that you would actually fund him?"

Garry Tan: "100%. In current form, 100%. I had a managing partner meeting the other day, and that's actually one of the example questions we ask ourselves to figure out whether we're on the right track." 

"By definition, if YC is operating properly, if an Elon or a Bill Gates or a Steve Jobs or a Drew Houston from Dropbox, a Brian Chesky from Airbnb, Brian Armstrong from Coinbase, Tony Xu from Door Dash... if someone like that walks into our office, can we say yes to them in 10 minutes? And if that answer is no, actually I'd have to rewrite everything. We'd have to retool everything. That is almost the only question that really matters when it comes to whether YC is doing well or not."

There are bull and bear takes on both sides, but the multiple compression is striking. Shared savings occur when an out of network (OON) claim is administered by a 3d party, e.g. formerly Multiplan, now called Claritev, it negotiates or recommends a lower fee for the OON services and Claritev then shares the “savings” (the delta between the charges and initial payment) w/ UHC.

text:
Today we are starting the rollout of Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC) for vercel.​com

DBSC makes it impossible to steal session cookies from a device. So, if you install info-stealer malware (e.g. through a supply chain attack), that malware can not steal your vercel.​com session.

Malware can still do bad things while residing on the device. But the abuse we are seeing in practice separates the stealing from the eventual abuse, and DBSC effectively prevents this.

DBSC works by storing a private key in your device's TPM (the same device that the fingerprint sensor or similar biometric devices on your laptop or phone uses) and using that key to sign your cookie. The private key can never be retrieved ever again. Not by us, not by you, not by the malware.

Every website should use DBSC but given how new of a technology it is, we still need to build more experience in rolling it out. In our case there were lots of special cases for things like oauth apps that we needed to resolve. This is also why we are taking a slow approach to the rollout.

DBSC is currently only supported by Chrome on Mac and Windows. We are also working on a kind of polyfill for other browsers. However, the polyfill is less secure and we would love to see broader browser adoption.

There is a related technology called DPoP which is essentially the same but for apps that run on your device. We're in the process of shipping this for Vercel CLI. Ideally, all CLIs and apps would adopt this technology. Luckily rolling out DPoP is much easier than DBSC and it does not depend on browser vendor support.

🚨BREAKING: Over 2,500 people on Michigan’s voter rolls are listed as 110 years old or older, according to a new complaint filed with state officials.

The Public Interest Legal Foundation identified roughly 2,461 registrations whose recorded birth years would make the voters at least 110. One entry lists a birth year of 1823 — 14 years before Michigan became a state.

The complaint says some of these records have stayed on the rolls for years despite prior alerts. Michigan’s own auditor general previously flagged hundreds of entries with birthdates older than 122, which officials have attributed in part to placeholder years used when old paper records were digitized. 

The findings land as Michigan continues large-scale cleanup of inactive and outdated registrations under Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson. Critics argue the continued presence of these extreme ages shows gaps in list maintenance ahead of the midterms.

Today, I’m sharing my first letter to the KMNO community as CEO

Since joining @kamino , I’ve been asked a version of the same question by longtime KMNO holders and people getting to know us for the first time. As Kamino grows, where does the value we create go?

It’s a fair question, particularly as we work to bring Kamino into banks, brokerages and wallets, through which our goal is to allow millions of people to earn on their capital or borrow against assets they already own.

The answer starts with how Kamino was built. The Kamino Foundation owns the intellectual property and receives all revenue, including revenue from institutional partnerships. KMNO is the only token. The founders, our investors, the team and I have our upside tied to the same token our community holds. None of us has a separate equity allocation.

What we do with the revenue matters, too. We’re committing at least $20 million over the next two years to expand the assets people can use on Kamino, and bring Kamino's credit and liquidity infrastructure to more of the platforms consumers already use today.

I wrote my first letter to KMNO holders to put those decisions on the record. I also share why I chose to make most of my own KMNO allocation vest only when it reaches and sustains a series of valuation milestones.

One Kamino. One KMNO.

BILL ACKMAN SAYS HE DOESN'T SEE A "ROARING 20S" BUBBLE IN THE STOCK MARKET

He was asked about Elliott Management's warning that today's market looks like the 1920s run-up to the Great Depression, and he pushed back hard.

"I don't see a roaring 20s in the stock market. If anything, this year earnings expectations have gone up meaningfully and the multiple is actually reasonably low relative to the growth inherent in the markets."

Ackman said the froth is in private markets and venture, though "a lot of it is justified." He pointed to fintech Ramp as an example, saying that if he were at American Express $AXP, "I would be concerned."

Where he does see excess is one-day options, heavy leverage and "a lot of money betting on the outcome of sports."

He also isn't worried about pushback on AI data centers slowing things down. "It's a global race for superintelligence. We don't want to get there second. That's existential to the United States."

text:
Analyst: Suspected North Korean Hackers Moved $1.46M via Jupiter Lend and Circle Bridge; Jupiter Says Funds Remain Traceable

On-chain analyst @FabianoSolana reported that suspected North Korean hackers moved approximately $1.46 million through Jupiter Lend and Circle’s cross-chain bridge. Funds from an FBI-flagged Solana wallet (AffzFD) were routed through roughly 35 intermediary wallets, consolidated, and deposited into Jupiter Lend before a new wallet withdrew a similar amount minutes later. The funds were then swapped into USDC, bridged through Noble and dYdX, and returned to Solana. The analyst reported 16 outbound transfers totaling $1,463,410 and 19 inbound transfers totaling $1,463,400, with no funds frozen.

Jupiter COO Kash Dhanda clarified that the attackers only deposited and withdrew funds through Jupiter Lend, unlike an earlier Aave incident involving borrowing non-freezable assets against stolen stablecoins. He said the funds remained fully traceable through LP tokens, with wallet associations preserved, and that Jupiter’s security team monitored the activity in real time. As of publication, Circle had not publicly addressed the transfers or explained why the funds were not frozen.

text:
Big news from @AnthropicAI  on verifiable LLM inference, with an exciting connection to Pearl’s proof of useful work.

Two orthogonal questions:
• Did the model you paid for actually produce this response?
• Was computational work performed?

Anthropic reports that generating inference proofs currently takes ~70–95× the GPU time of ordinary inference. Pearl’s PoUW, on the contrary, adds negligible overhead. These costs buy different guarantees. Proving correct inference doesn’t automatically establish proof of work and the other way around. But the two are deeply complementary. Verifiable inference could certify which model produced an answer, while Pearl׳s PoUW only certifies that a computation has been done.

As inference proofs get more practical, that combination could make AI easier to trust and more economical to provide.

text:
我想明白了这件事情，产能卖到 2029 年，Lumentum 为什么偏偏现在把自己卖掉？

Evercore 在电话会前就问了这个问题：既然产能都卖光了，为什么要卖？管理层的回答是"考虑过其他选项"，以及和 Marvell 一起能更好地做 scale-up、scale-in。这解释了为什么选 Marvell，没有解释为什么是现在。

下面是我的推理。这是推断，公司没有这么说过。

【一、CPO 改变的不是需求，是谁来买】

可插拔模块时代，Lumentum 把 EML 卖给几十家模块厂（旭创、新易盛等）。客户分散，模块厂自己定义不了激光器，议价权在 Lumentum 手里。

CPO 时代，激光器从模块里搬出来，变成外置光源，买家变成少数几个掌握交换芯片或 XPU 的平台方：Nvidia、博通、AMD 和几家云厂商。

这个变化已经在数字里了：Lumentum 最大客户的收入占比，一年内从 15.4% 升到 26.6%。

【二、平台方的议价工具，比模块厂多得多】

· 规格由买方定。CPO 光源采用 ELSFP 标准化可插拔外形，越标准化，越接近按规格采购的零件，换供应商越容易。

· 买方主动扶持第二供应商。Nvidia 3 月同时给 Lumentum 和 Coherent 各投了 $20 亿，拿到的是非独占产能权。Coherent 计划把自有 InP 激光器产能翻一倍，到 2027 年底再翻一倍，超高功率 CPO 光源预计 2026 年第四季度开始量产。

· 买方可以自己做。博通有自己的 InP 晶圆厂，Intel 也在推 InP 硅光。

· 价值重心转移。在 CPO 系统里，价值集中在交换芯片、XPU 和台积电的封装，激光器只是平台方成本清单上的一行。

【三、所以现在是 Lumentum 议价权的顶点】

眼下，CPO 超高功率光源只有 Lumentum 一家通过 Nvidia 认证，产能卖到 2029 年，EML 价格还在涨，估值处在高位（传闻前市盈率约 42 倍预期盈利，5 年均值约 30 倍）。

往后看，第二供应商起来、标准化推进、买家集中度上升，议价权会慢慢向买方转移。量不一定少（scale-up 用光替代的是铜，是新增市场），但单价和利润率的天花板会降下来。

在议价权最强、估值最高的时候，把"供应商"的身份换成"平台"的股权，这是我认为最能解释交易时机的逻辑。

【四、几个需要说清的点】

· 收股票，说明不是套现，而是换位。Lumentum 股东将持有合并后约 33%，继续分享"电+光"平台的成长。这也是现实约束：Marvell 账上只有约 $39 亿现金，$1,150 亿的交易只能用股票。

· 短期市场和长期逻辑在打架。11/2 当天 MRVL 收 $171.41，4.5 股只值约 $771，远低于 $1,132 的标题价，LITE 收盘还比这个价值低约 11%。市场在为稀释、长达 18 个月的交割期和整合风险打折扣。如果整合顺利、CPO 按时放量，这个折价就是长期持有者的机会；反过来，折价也可能继续扩大。

· 时间表有不确定性。主流预期 scale-up CPO 在 2027 年下半年量产、2028 年部署，也有业内观点认为要等到 2030 年以后。如果铜撑得更久，可插拔 EML 的好日子更长，那现在卖就卖早了。

【结论】

这不是"生意变差了才卖"，也不是高位套现，而是在 CPO 把议价权交给少数平台方之前，用稀缺性换一个好价格，并且把自己变成平台的一部分。双方都在赌 CPO 时代到来：

Marvell 赌的是拿到光源后能和 Nvidia、博通平起平坐，Lumentum 股东赌的是平台的位置比供应商的位置更值钱，而且他们选择留在牌桌上。

text:
Spending apps forget what you taught them because your rules live in someone else's database or a localStorage blob. And when an agent meets an unnamed hex address on-chain, it either guesses or gives up.

I built RecallSpend for the @tatum_io x @WalrusProtocol Total Recall hackathon on @SuiNetwork — a Sui spending tracker with no database:

• One-time sync via Tatum Sui GraphQL (6 credits, 1 bulk write). Every page load after that reads strictly from Walrus Memory for 0 credits.
• Every spend, human correction, and agent payment is an immutable, append-only line in Walrus Memory. Corrections never overwrite observations, so the app always knows what it thought before you taught it otherwise.
• When it meets an unknown merchant, you can correct it for free or let the agent buy the label for 0.01 USDC over MPP on Sui Mainnet.
• Payment and memory writes are split in two steps, and proveUsdcTransfer verifies the 0.01 USDC transfer on Sui before the label is written.
• Generalisation (0% → 100%) is scored only on held-out repeat payments you never touched.
• Ask Memory cites the exact Walrus lines behind every answer, with no LLM in the loop.

The live app is pre-loaded with a synced demo wallet and a pre-funded agent wallet so you can test a real 0.01 USDC mainnet lookup in one click.

text:
Major Developer Documentation Platform GitBook Hit by AI Agent-Driven Attack, Crypto Projects' Docs Affected

GitBook reported that attackers used AI agents to gain unauthorized access to some of its infrastructure credentials at 1:00 p.m. EST on November 2. The company detected and blocked the attack, temporarily suspending some services. Potentially exposed data includes integration tokens, Git Sync secrets, API tokens, and visitor questions submitted to GitBook Assistant. No evidence of content modification has been found. GitBook rotated all infrastructure credentials and secrets, revoked all customer API tokens, and advised users to rotate third-party credentials and re-authenticate GitBook MCP connections. By 10:21 a.m. EST on November 3, its app, API, and published docs were accessible again, though some services remained degraded. A full post-incident report is planned.

Previously, trade[XYZ] reported unauthorized activity involving its GitBook documentation, which it later restored, and warned users against clicking links during the investigation. PancakeSwap temporarily took its documentation site offline as a precaution following the GitBook security incident and redirected documentation links to its official homepage.

When I get error messages I just copy paste them in with no comment, usually that fixes it. The code grows beyond my usual comprehension, I'd have to really read through it for a while. Sometimes the LLMs can't fix a bug so I just work around it or ask for random changes until it goes away. It's not too bad for throwaway weekend projects, but still quite amusing. I'm building a project or webapp, but it's not really coding - I just see stuff, say stuff, run stuff, and copy paste stuff, and it mostly works.

@AnthropicAI’s impressive work on FlashProve is a real signal for the value of @prlnet’s technology in the toolbox of  provable inference (PI).

FlashProve proves inference correctness post-hoc. Moving it to real-time proof-of-inference requires time-stamping, which is what blockchains were made for.. 

The reality is that AI verification often cares about what a datacenter DIDN’T run. Correct inference proofs don’t rule out parallel, unmonitored workloads. @prlnet’s Pearl-GEMM protocol anchors the output to computation (FLOPs). Paired with PI, it could help bound capacity available for unauthorized training, and provide a “model-tracing” audit for agentic workloads.

Pearl is uniquely positioned to build the work-accounting layer of PI infrastructure.

text:
Big news from @AnthropicAI  on verifiable LLM inference, with an exciting connection to Pearl’s proof of useful work.

Two orthogonal questions:
• Did the model you paid for actually produce this response?
• Was computational work performed?

Anthropic reports that generating inference proofs currently takes ~70–95× the GPU time of ordinary inference. Pearl’s PoUW, on the contrary, adds negligible overhead. These costs buy different guarantees. Proving correct inference doesn’t automatically establish proof of work and the other way around. But the two are deeply complementary. Verifiable inference could certify which model produced an answer, while Pearl׳s PoUW only certifies that a computation has been done.

As inference proofs get more practical, that combination could make AI easier to trust and more economical to provide.

PULSE (also called Delta weight sync) has become one of the most important ideas in RL infrastructure this year. Our paper, posted on February 3, explained why it loses nothing. At RL learning rates, about 99% of each step's weight updates disappear in the BF16 cast, so the inference workers never see them.

Since then, @huggingface has built Delta Weight Sync for TRL and vLLM on that argument. @FireworksAI_HQ cites PULSE, and its ARCv3 compressor now makes the updates even smaller.

This week @humansand reported pausing inference for only about 220 milliseconds per update on Blackwell GPUs.

PULSE has now been accepted at AXIOM, a @NeurIPSConf 2026 workshop.

Anthropic has a 15-person chip design team and has told investors they are using Claude to design chips faster than Nvidia or AMD

Earlier this year at GTC, Nvidia’s Chief Scienst Bill Dally told Jeff Dean how Nvidia uses AI to speed up the chip design process:

▫️trained an LLM on all proprietary internal Nvidia docs over past 30+ years (junior employees query it instead of interrupting senior designers)

▫️one AI tool ports Nvidia’s cell library to a new semiconductor process and does it in only one night (used to take 10 employees up to 8 months, or 80 total person-months)

▫️since the 1950s, there’s been a classic chip design problem of where to place look ahead stages in a chain (AI is coming up with solutions using “bizarre designs thay no human” would think of)

▫️agentic AI systems are doing a ton of exploration…testing parameters spaces…suggesting new approaches…running architecture experiments 

▫️verification process is laborious but AI able to do it at fraction of time (compresses time from design to tape-out, with TSMC making chip)

Dally says it’s still a long way from end-to-end chip design but imagines a world where one master AI agents manages multiple sub-agents (similar to the current human-led process).

text:
Clanker: Reboot.

2 years ago (almost to the day), Clanker was born over on the original Farcaster app. The idea was simple: Make it possible for anyone to launch a token just by posting on the timeline and tagging @clanker_world. 

The timing was right, and it caught on like wildfire. Suddenly, even people who never thought they’d launch a token were trying it out in the feed. (I even clanked my first meme token on day 1 to see how it all worked. If you search hard, you can probably find it.)

Over the ensuing year, Clanker went on a genny run, expanding from Fc to the X feed and becoming the highest volume launchpad on @base by far, birthing some of the most iconic tokens & token communities of that era, including BNKR, DRB, FAIR & more. 

So many builders on Farcaster & beyond turned to Clanker to bootstrap their ideas & find their first 1,000 true fans. Legends like @0FJAKE, @AtownBrown, @david_tomu and @darkohh clanked tokens for their projects. Some, like @MLeeJr, even took it upon themselves to clank tokens for OTHER people’s projects.

And when @netnose and I decided to build a gacha app for creator discovery, we clanked our native token on day one too.

There’s just always been something fundamentally OP about clanking tokens right in the feed. Social graph integration remains undefeated in the attention economy. 

But despite all this pedigree & lore, Clanker has had… a rough time lately, to say the least. Between early founder drama, the sale to Farcaster and the eventual handoff to Neynar, Clanker’s been like a teenager who hasn’t been allowed to finish a full year at the same school. How can you even make friends like that?

Hopefully, that all changes today.

Clanker is in good hands now with @masknetwork (stewards of Firefly and Lens Protocol), and they’ve partnered with one of the best engineering teams in the space to give Clanker a much-needed Reboot. More on that soon, but in the meantime…

I’m excited to announce that I’ve accepted the role of Clanker CEO and will be taking on the challenge of guiding our beloved tokenbot back to its former glory.

Transparently, this wasn’t a decision I took lightly. I’ve been self-employed since I was 17, and always preferred to work on things I founded myself. But Clanker has held a very special place in my heart since day 1, and I feel like the little guy’s been a victim of circumstance for much of the past 18 months. He deserves a second chance at romance, and I’m honored to be the one to lead the charge. 

I’m also grateful to everyone who helped make Clanker what it is today. To Proxy and Jack for the founder energy, to Base and Farcaster for backing the ecosystem, to communities like DRB and Bankr for keeping it alive, and to @ProfWerder & @age_shulman for their stewardship too. The fact that this little tokenbot has survived all these seasons is crazy in its own right. We stand on the shoulders of giants.

Much more to come from me soon, but here are my main priorities to start:

- Reboot and refresh the Clanker brand without losing its special je ne sais quoi.

- Work with our socials guru @stanisloou to keep comms fresh and clean.

- Work with our engineering team to bring clanker features up to parity with modern launchpads (stock pairs, new chains and even day one support for _______)

- Rebuild the trust that has been lost with both builders & trenchers through all these transitions.

- Show up for OG communities who are still here building and shipping two years later.

- Bring new launch energy back to Clanker & back to the feed, where distribution is built-in by default. 

So if you’re looking to launch a funny meme, a clever stock pair, or an app coin to bootstrap your project, I want to help you succeed. 

Same goes if you’re a builder with an idea to build on top of clanker protocol; the energy here has always been collaborative and that won’t change. 

My DMs are open and we can win together. 

Let’s press REBOOT and run it back turbo. 

Clank Clank!

text: Lear 60 will be airplane equivalent of the $1 Italian Villa.
author: PallerJohn
author_name: J O H N P A L L Ξ R | pallΞr.Ξth (🦬,🦄)
quoted_text:
Long post worth the read. I have a close friend who flies private jets. He flew Lear 60 for over 15 years and now flies a Gulfstream. This is a copy and paste of his response to me asking him if he thought Ice was the issue. 

“We always fly in ridiculous cold temperatures.” 

“Usually you get the bad ice when the temperatures are like 0 to negative 20.  Believe it or not,  there's a point where it gets too cold for ice.   At negative 40, you pretty much can't get ice.   Besides that,  the airplane is equipped with hot wings and hot tail.”

“I flew the Lear 60 for like 15 years.   It's a no joke airplane and probably the most dangerous airplane I've ever flown.   It has a super critical wing.   The airflow has to be perfect.   When it gets into rough air and turbulence,  it will easily stall.   It has stalled on me at 41,000 feet just because we got into some turbulence.   (On the way to Palm Beach as a matter of fact. ) we recovered and got her flying again around 30,000 ft.   Scary

But here's the problem.   This airplane has a terrible coffin corner.   (At high altitudes)  what that means is,  you fly in a really narrow window where if you lose 20 knots,  it stalls.   And if you gain 20 knots,  it goes into overspeed.   The air goes supersonic over the wing and it goes into a high speed stall,  or worse,  a Mach tuck.   

So if you stall,  the normal recovery is to push the yoke forward to lower the nose and gain air speed again.   At low altitude,  you can push really hard and recover quickly.   But in the 60... if you push hard,  it will gain air speed and go into a high speed stall,  it doesn't take much.   It's very sensitive.  The 60 has super short wings that don't make much lift.   So then you high speed stall,  and the computer is yelling at you... OVERSPEED!   So then you pull back and enter a low speed stall.   And you go back and forth trying to keep it in the air speed window.   

This whole thing is pretty scary.   And you should recover basically by using your finger tips using super small corrections.   You can't over do it.   If you try to muscle the recovery, she gets mad and will become unrecoverable.  If she enters a mach tuck.  You're done.”

“I taught the Lear 60 to other pilots and mentored them.   I told them... this airplane has a soul and it's trying to kill you.   Do not ever try to top the weather.   Don't go over a thunderstorm.   Go around it.   If it means a half hour longer,  then do it.   Going over the thunderstorm will go into turbulence that you might not recover from.   

These pilots went right over a thunderstorm.   I think it stalled which caused them to drop down into the thunderstorm and ended up in mach tuck.   They picked up so much speed that it ripped off the horizontal stabilizer.   At that point... chuck Yeager can't fix it.   

These same pilots did something similar a couple months ago.   ATC got mad at them.   They poked the bear one too many times.   

This is not a beginner airplane.   The Gulfstream would never do this.   It has HUGE margins of error and won't stall like that.   But then again... it's got HUGE wings.   It's a pussy cat.  

The Gulfstream is like driving a 4 wheeler.   The Lear 60 is like riding a uni cycle.”

PULSE (also called Delta weight sync) has become one of the most important ideas in RL infrastructure this year. Our paper, posted on February 3, explained why it loses nothing. At RL learning rates, about 99% of each step's weight updates disappear in the BF16 cast, so the inference workers never see them.

Since then, @huggingface has built Delta Weight Sync for TRL and vLLM on that argument. @FireworksAI_HQ cites PULSE, and its ARCv3 compressor now makes the updates even smaller.

This week @humansand reported pausing inference for only about 220 milliseconds per update on Blackwell GPUs.

PULSE has now been accepted at AXIOM, a @NeurIPSConf 2026 workshop.

quoted_text:
In my 20’s, I used to work on Wall Street. 

People my age now (45) said they were working 70, 80, 90 hours a week for their families…but all their families actually wanted was their presence.

They didn’t understand why their families resented how much they worked when they lived in a nice house, and their kids went to private schools. 

It was just the world we all lived in. We knew nothing else.

I decided early in my startup journey that wasn’t going to be me.

My co-founders and I have always had a policy of quitting at 5 or 5:30.

By that, I mean:

> Shut off my laptop
> No more work talk
> Go home to my family
 
Frequently I’m out even earlier - 3-5, depending on whether I want to do something with the kids.

I rarely travel for work and don’t entertain for work. 

My family life gives me energy for my work. 
My work gives me energy for my family life. 

I'm trying to stay not burnt out and excited about this for several decades.
 
Can every founder choose this?

Maybe not everybody, but more people have the choice than realize they do.

There is great reward that comes from designing a business around the life you want.

text:
The Binance incident exposed at least three mistakes that were entirely avoidable:

1. Development and operations environments were not fully isolated. Anyone with production access should operate from a dedicated machine used for nothing else, with no third-party software installed on it — coding, chat, and web browsing all belong on a separate device.

2. The operations stack had no meaningful 2FA. A single key was enough to operate production services, which means that once the key leaked, the attacker had full production access. The right approach is to run production operations through something like AWS's browser-based Session Manager, with a hardware security key enforced as a second factor, so that a single leaked credential is never enough to constitute a breach.

3. The MPC multisig existed in name only. The signing parties performed no substantive independent verification, so compromising one node brought down the entire scheme — a multisig that behaves no differently from a single signature. Multisig only works when the signers are mutually distrustful: each party must independently verify the transaction itself, rather than trusting whatever request comes from upstream.

None of these require sophisticated technology. What was missing was discipline.

This made my GPU bill go from $36,000/mo to $7,000/mo

- $3,000/mo - consolidated my servers, cancelled Digital Ocean and Linode and moved everything to Hetzner saving about $3,000/mo

- $1100/mo - analyzed my Backblaze B2 server backups, I had infinite versioning and lifecycle policies, that's reduced now to 30 days, this literally pushed the bill from $1,200/mo to $26/mo, about 50x cheaper! I had essentially versions of files for all my servers for over a decade, crazy!

- $400/mo - similarly added Lifecycle Policies to my Cloudflare R2 bucket for Photo AI, pics are automatically put in cheaper Infrequent Access after 90 days, there was years of photos in there so this reduced the R2 bill from $1,200/mo to $800/mo

- $118/mo - Claude analyzed all my Cloudflare Domain registrations, lots of domains I didn't use and didn't make sense to keep paying for, lots of things that also don't really make sense anymore in a post-AGI world, renewals for .io TLD are now $50/year which adds up fast!

- $100/mo - Claude also analyzed my Claude subscription (yes!) and discovered I don't even use the Max 20x plan limits, so I downgraded from $200/mo to $100/mo

Even including Photo AI, I have now cut my costs by 90% from last year, getting me close to my biz expenses amount from a decade ago when I started building things

Costs slowly creep up over the years and you don't realize all the things you're spending on but AI is nice to help you figure all that out (also in your personal life!)

Clanker: Reboot.

2 years ago (almost to the day), Clanker was born over on the original Farcaster app. The idea was simple: Make it possible for anyone to launch a token just by posting on the timeline and tagging @clanker_world. 

The timing was right, and it caught on like wildfire. Suddenly, even people who never thought they’d launch a token were trying it out in the feed. (I even clanked my first meme token on day 1 to see how it all worked. If you search hard, you can probably find it.)

Over the ensuing year, Clanker went on a genny run, expanding from Fc to the X feed and becoming the highest volume launchpad on @base by far, birthing some of the most iconic tokens & token communities of that era, including BNKR, DRB, FAIR & more. 

So many builders on Farcaster & beyond turned to Clanker to bootstrap their ideas & find their first 1,000 true fans. Legends like @0FJAKE, @AtownBrown, @david_tomu and @darkohh clanked tokens for their projects. Some, like @MLeeJr, even took it upon themselves to clank tokens for OTHER people’s projects.

And when @netnose and I decided to build a gacha app for creator discovery, we clanked our native token on day one too.

There’s just always been something fundamentally OP about clanking tokens right in the feed. Social graph integration remains undefeated in the attention economy. 

But despite all this pedigree & lore, Clanker has had… a rough time lately, to say the least. Between early founder drama, the sale to Farcaster and the eventual handoff to Neynar, Clanker’s been like a teenager who hasn’t been allowed to finish a full year at the same school. How can you even make friends like that?

Hopefully, that all changes today.

Clanker is in good hands now with @masknetwork (stewards of Firefly and Lens Protocol), and they’ve partnered with one of the best engineering teams in the space to give Clanker a much-needed Reboot. More on that soon, but in the meantime…

I’m excited to announce that I’ve accepted the role of Clanker CEO and will be taking on the challenge of guiding our beloved tokenbot back to its former glory.

Transparently, this wasn’t a decision I took lightly. I’ve been self-employed since I was 17, and always preferred to work on things I founded myself. But Clanker has held a very special place in my heart since day 1, and I feel like the little guy’s been a victim of circumstance for much of the past 18 months. He deserves a second chance at romance, and I’m honored to be the one to lead the charge. 

I’m also grateful to everyone who helped make Clanker what it is today. To Proxy and Jack for the founder energy, to Base and Farcaster for backing the ecosystem, to communities like DRB and Bankr for keeping it alive, and to @ProfWerder & @age_shulman for their stewardship too. The fact that this little tokenbot has survived all these seasons is crazy in its own right. We stand on the shoulders of giants.

Much more to come from me soon, but here are my main priorities to start:

- Reboot and refresh the Clanker brand without losing its special je ne sais quoi.

- Work with our socials guru @stanisloou to keep comms fresh and clean.

- Work with our engineering team to bring clanker features up to parity with modern launchpads (stock pairs, new chains and even day one support for _______)

- Show up for OG communities who are still here building and shipping two years later.

- Bring new launch energy back to Clanker & back to the feed, where distribution is built-in by default. 

So if you’re looking to launch a funny meme, a clever stock pair, or an app coin to bootstrap your project, I want to help you succeed. 

Same goes if you’re a builder with an idea to build on top of clanker protocol; the energy here has always been collaborative and that won’t change. 

My DMs are open and we can win together. 

Let’s press REBOOT and run it back turbo.

text:
Taylor Hornby (@DefuseSec) on the state of AI-assisted software audits: 

Current models are great at auditing, and everyone needs to be doing it. The two biggest problems that still need solving are: 

(a) models are not good at properly understanding an issue’s severity, so there is still a lot of manual work to validate what the AI finds (this is the next thing I want to work on), and 

(b) defenders need access to the best models without cyber safeguards in order to audit their own code. 

Frontier labs need to do a better job of letting legitimate security research and auditing through the safeguards, and of providing AI audits and patching support to open-source projects. Anthropic’s Fable safeguards’ initial refusals to work on pretty much anything cryptography-related may have ultimately done more harm than good, since they blocked legitimate defensive research. 

The situation has gotten better now that Anthropic has allowed users in their Cyber Verification Program to run Mythos on security tasks.

text:
Binance Hack Timeline: How Attackers Compromised Three Engineers to Access Wallet Signing Service

WuBlockchain mapped the attack timeline based on Binance’s preliminary investigation. In June, Wallet DevOps Engineer A downloaded a tampered Homebrew installer while setting up an AI coding tool. Although Binance detected the incident, replaced the device and rotated credentials, information about the engineer and colleagues was exposed. In September, Engineer B downloaded a malicious code repository during a fake job interview, compromising his work computer. On October 20, attackers used the compromised device and an internal AI tool to gain control over Engineers A and C, discovering a container deployment permission token on A’s computer. On October 29, they accessed C’s computer, used credentials stolen from A to deploy a container and execute a malicious script, and ultimately initiated unauthorized asset transfers through Binance’s internal wallet signing service.

text: Clanker: Reboot
author: juliezize
quoted_text:
Clanker: Reboot.

2 years ago (almost to the day), Clanker was born over on the original Farcaster app. The idea was simple: Make it possible for anyone to launch a token just by posting on the timeline and tagging @clanker_world. 

The timing was right, and it caught on like wildfire. Suddenly, even people who never thought they’d launch a token were trying it out in the feed. (I even clanked my first meme token on day 1 to see how it all worked. If you search hard, you can probably find it.)

Over the ensuing year, Clanker went on a genny run, expanding from Fc to the X feed and becoming the highest volume launchpad on @base by far, birthing some of the most iconic tokens & token communities of that era, including BNKR, DRB, FAIR & more. 

So many builders on Farcaster & beyond turned to Clanker to bootstrap their ideas & find their first 1,000 true fans. Legends like @0FJAKE, @AtownBrown, @david_tomu and @darkohh clanked tokens for their projects. Some, like @MLeeJr, even took it upon themselves to clank tokens for OTHER people’s projects.

And when @netnose and I decided to build a gacha app for creator discovery, we clanked our native token on day one too.

There’s just always been something fundamentally OP about clanking tokens right in the feed. Social graph integration remains undefeated in the attention economy. 

But despite all this pedigree & lore, Clanker has had… a rough time lately, to say the least. Between early founder drama, the sale to Farcaster and the eventual handoff to Neynar, Clanker’s been like a teenager who hasn’t been allowed to finish a full year at the same school. How can you even make friends like that?

Hopefully, that all changes today.

Clanker is in good hands now with @masknetwork (stewards of Firefly and Lens Protocol), and they’ve partnered with one of the best engineering teams in the space to give Clanker a much-needed Reboot. More on that soon, but in the meantime…

I’m excited to announce that I’ve accepted the role of Clanker CEO and will be taking on the challenge of guiding our beloved tokenbot back to its former glory.

Transparently, this wasn’t a decision I took lightly. I’ve been self-employed since I was 17, and always preferred to work on things I founded myself. But Clanker has held a very special place in my heart since day 1, and I feel like the little guy’s been a victim of circumstance for much of the past 18 months. He deserves a second chance at romance, and I’m honored to be the one to lead the charge. 

I’m also grateful to everyone who helped make Clanker what it is today. To Proxy and Jack for the founder energy, to Base and Farcaster for backing the ecosystem, to communities like DRB and Bankr for keeping it alive, and to @ProfWerder & @age_shulman for their stewardship too. The fact that this little tokenbot has survived all these seasons is crazy in its own right. We stand on the shoulders of giants.

Much more to come from me soon, but here are my main priorities to start:

- Reboot and refresh the Clanker brand without losing its special je ne sais quoi.

- Work with our socials guru @stanisloou to keep comms fresh and clean.

- Work with our engineering team to bring clanker features up to parity with modern launchpads (stock pairs, new chains and even day one support for _______)

- Rebuild the trust that has been lost with both builders & trenchers through all these transitions.

- Show up for OG communities who are still here building and shipping two years later.

- Bring new launch energy back to Clanker & back to the feed, where distribution is built-in by default. 

So if you’re looking to launch a funny meme, a clever stock pair, or an app coin to bootstrap your project, I want to help you succeed. 

Same goes if you’re a builder with an idea to build on top of clanker protocol; the energy here has always been collaborative and that won’t change. 

My DMs are open and we can win together. 

Let’s press REBOOT and run it back turbo. 

Clank Clank!

text:
I am happy to share FlashProve: our performant open-source prototype for provable inference. We believe that this has significant implications for security, pacing AI development, integrity guarantees, and more. 

FlashProve allows a provider to commit to model weights, and then prove that replies originate from the committed model.  The proof leaks no information about the weights, and the verifier can efficiently verify it on consumer hardware. 

Our library is performant, proving a 400B parameter MoE model at 100 tok/s. We have open-sourced the associated code and Lean formalization. We hope that it catalyzes further progress in verification of inference, and look forward to seeing it.
author: GiacomoFenzi
quoted_text:
New Anthropic research: progress on provable inference for large language models.

Here, we introduce FlashProve. Building on established cryptographic techniques, FlashProve allows developers to verify whether a given response came from a given AI model. It’s substantially more efficient than prior open-source methods for doing so. 

These proofs have a range of applications. They can, for instance, make it harder for attackers to hijack a chat, or enable safety evaluators to verify that the model they’re testing is the same one being served to customers.

For our full write-up, see here: https://t.co/OIZWPb6QZa

Further progress in provable inference will likely be an important part of improving trust in AI deployment. To that end, we're open-sourcing FlashProve’s code, here: https://t.co/7ky3Ir8V06

We’re grateful to our collaborators: Alessandro Chiesa, @GiacomoFenzi, @gwberg95, @miranda__christ, Rahul Dalal (https://t.co/pjWKLHWXyz) and Ben Mayer (@transmissions11).

text:
Again, if your systems are so simple and weak that a single employee's device can move the money, then you are fucked.

In fact, if you have a single critical system that can move all your money, then you are fucked.

Single points of failure will fuck you. Always.

I understand that being fucked is totally normal in this space.

But I refuse to pretend that it's okay.

It's absolutely not.

It's honestly this mindset that leads to so many of these hacks. Binance and Bitget are unique in that they actually do have relatively complex systems with a lot of moving pieces. It's actually not as simple as one device -> one box -> all the money (as much as CT is making it seem like it is 🤮)

But if we go back to other recent incidents, the "limit access to critical systems and hope no one gets malware" has resulted in, literally, billions stolen.

Limiting access doesn't replace EDR. EDR doesn't mean youll detect every single malicious thing (or react in perfect time.) Only doing short lived hardware MFA tokens doesn't mean they magically cant follow you into the systems (or find a backdoor via a different vuln/0day.) And, certainly, assuming your employees wont get phished is never going to cut it when there are billions on the line.

You MUST assume that people and devices get popped and limit/eliminate the damage even if that happens.
